Executive summary
English version

Since 2012, the European Commission has requested the European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice
(CEPEJ) of the Council of Europe, to carry out a study aimed at analysing the situation of the judicial systems in
the EU member States based on the specific methodology developed and used by the CEPEJ for evaluating the
functioning of the judicial systems of the Council of Europe member States.
This study is based on collecting, processing, and analysing data and comments provided by the European Union
(EU) member States through:
  · selected data among those collected for the six CEPEJ evaluation cycles (years of reference of the data:
  2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022).
  ·    and specific questionnaires (for years of reference 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023, 2024)
This study will constitute one of the sources used by the European Commission for the “EU Justice Scoreboard”.
Structure of the study
Following the last proposed technical specifications provided in the framework of the Contribution Agreement
JUST-2025-IM-JACC/RIGH/1 “Service to support the annual publication of the EU Justice Scoreboard”, the study,
based on 2024 data and also their evolution in relation to 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022
and 2023 data, is structured in two main parts:
  the first part examines the judicial systems in the EU member States providing data tables per indicator for all
  member States;
 the second part contains country profiles for each EU member state separately, with a contextual analysis.
Main elements
The study, through the 8 indicators, provides an overview of the functioning of the justice system based on the
elements, selected by the European Commission (EC) and which, according to the CEPEJ, are essential to the
effectivity and quality of judicial systems.
Human resources
Different categories of judges (professional, occasional, non-professional) can contribute to the justice system.
The 2024 study focuses on professional judges sitting in courts and the European Union average for this category
of judges is 22,6 judges per 100 000 inhabitants (the median is 23,4 judges per 100 000 inhabitants). The lowest
number of professional judges per 100 000 inhabitants is 3.6 and the highest is 44,4. The average value has
slightly increased between 2023 and 2024 from 21,5 to 23,4.

It can be noted that compared with the previous cycle, the number of judges per 100 000 inhabitants increased
for more than 1% in 13 member States, whereas it decreased by more than 1% in 5 member States which
confirms the mentioned trend of increased median. The remaining countries have reported smaller changes in
numbers which can be interpreted as a normal fluctuation of human resources within a system.
This number depends considerably on the organisation of the judicial system and the existence of occasional
judges, non-professional judges or even Rechtspfleger.
The existence alongside professional judges of competent staff with defined functions and a recognised status is
essential for the quality and efficiency of a judicial system. A distinction is made between the five types of non-
judge staff:
- the "Rechtspfleger " function,
- the non-judge staff whose role is to assist judges directly,
- the staff responsible for administrative matters,
- the technical staff,
- and other types of non-judge staff that fall outside of all the categories mentioned above.
The analysis of data provided by the member States shows different trends for the average and median values.
Since 2014, the average number of non-judge staff per 100 000 inhabitants has increased around 5% while the
median increased even more (8%). Compared with the last cycle, the average increased 0,63% while the median
decreased by 1,33%. The EU median of the non-judge staff per 100 000 inhabitants is 59,4 with the lowest as 23,9
and highest as 158,8.
It is worth noting that 12 countries reported to have staff with "Rechspfleger " functions (or equivalent) among non-
judge staff.
Since 2020, the CEPEJ Study for the EU Justice Scoreboard includes prosecution services. The diversity in
activities of the prosecution services is evident and the number of prosecutors per 100 000 inhabitant varies in
European Union from minimum 2,9 to maximum 24 with an average and median of 11,4 prosecutors per 100 000
inhabitants. Compared to the previous cycle, both the average and median values increased by 1% and 7%
respectively.
The prosecutors are assisted in their work by non-prosecutor staff attached to the prosecutors' offices. Their
number varies largely in the member States from 0,9 to 46,68 non-prosecutor staff per 100 000 inhabitants with
an average 15,5 and median 14,5. Compared to the previous cycle, the average and median values are very
stable.
Regarding salaries of judges and public prosecutors, it could be noted that their absolute amounts vary largely
from state to state depending mostly on the economic situation and the level of the GDP per capita. From 2018
onward, nearly all states showed a consistent trend of salary increase, with 27% increase of average gross annual
salary of judges at the beginning of their career and 33% increase of average gross annual salary for judges of the
Supreme Court or the Highest Appellate Court. A similar trend is also observed with prosecutors, with 30%
increase of the average gross annual salary of public prosecutors at the beginning of their career and 36%
increase of the average gross annual salary of public prosecutors at the Supreme Court or the Highest Appellate
Instance.
When viewed in a national context, the judges at the beginning of career on average earn 2 times average annual
salary in their respective countries, whereas this ratio is a bit lower for public prosecutors - 1,7. A similar disparity
is observed among judges and prosecutors of the Supreme Court or the Highest Appellate Instance, where the
highest salary of a judge at the Supreme Court is on average 4,1 times higher than the average salary in the
country, while public prosecutors of the corresponding level earn 3,6 the average salary in the country.
Lawyers
The average number of lawyers per 100 000 inhabitants in the EU member States has generally shown an upward
trend since 2014. Between 2014 and 2024 the average number of lawyers in the EU member States increased by
15% and the median by 23%.
Although the southern states (such as Italy, Greece, Cyprus, Spain, Portugal etc.), but also Luxembourg appear to
have a higher number of lawyers per 100,000 inhabitants, the significant discrepancy in values, also reflected in
the ratio of lawyers to professional judges, suggests considerable heterogeneity in the roles and tasks performed.
Judicial organisation
The study distinguishes three types of courts:
-    courts of general jurisdiction that deal with any issues which are not attributed to specialised courts – their
enumeration is made as legal entities for first, second and third instances;
-    specialised courts of first instance and those of higher instances (second and/or third instance combined),
also considered as legal entities;
-    courts, at all levels and of first instance, as geographic locations.
Since 2014, 12 member States have reduced their number of geographical locations, 3 have the same number
and 11 increased it. Between the last two cycles, 3 member States increased, and 3 countries reduced the
number of courts' geographic locations.
The geographical locations per 100 000 inhabitants have decreased in most of the member States (the median
was 1,54 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2014; 1,38 in 2016 and 1,45 in 2024 which is -4,5 % decrease).
As regards the distribution of the disputes between legal entities, all the EU member States except for the Czech
Republic and Hungary have specialised courts of first instance.
The most frequent types of specialised courts in EU states are those that deal with administrative cases (exist in
all but 5 member states), labour disputes; (exist in 11 member states) and commercial cases (exist in 11 member
states).
Significant number of countries have also other not mentioned specialised courts (11 member states). While the
majority of countries have few types of specialised courts there are some that have many specialised courts for
different matters like Spain, Portugal, Cyprus, France but also Austria, and Italy.

Portugal, France and Cyprus also have large number of specialised courts of 1st instance compared with all
courts of 1st instance (75%, 84% and 63% respectively). There are few more countries with many different types
of specialised courts, but they qualified them as “other” so they cannot be easily compared with other systems.

Since 2020 the data on the higher instances specialised, courts were collected. Expectedly, their number is
smaller than the 1st instance. Few countries have many specialised courts dealing with different cases at the
higher instances. In most of the other countries that have higher instance specialised courts, they deal with the
administrative matters (19 countries). There are also some higher instance military courts as well. There are also 4
countries that have specialised courts at 1st instance but no specialised courts on higher instances.
ADR - Alternative Dispute Resolution measures
In various EU member States, the use of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) is now widely accepted among the
public and legal professionals. It contributes to the improvement of effectiveness of justice by providing court
users with alternatives to a regular judicial procedure.
There are different types of ADR in the member States:
Mediation: refers to a voluntary process in a non-binding private dispute settlement in which an impartial and
independent third party assists the parties in facilitating discussions aiming to resolve their difficulties and to
reach an agreement.
Court-related mediation: in this type of mediation, there’s always an intervention of a judge and of a prosecutor
who facilitates, advises, decides and/or approves the procedure.
Conciliation: the main objective of a conciliator is to reconcile, most of the time he/she will do so by seeking
concessions. He/she may make suggestions to the parties aimed to settle a dispute. The conciliator has more
power and plays a more proactive role in comparison with the mediator.
Arbitration: the parties choose a neutral third party - an arbitrator whose final decision is binding. The parties may
present evidence and testimonies to the arbitrators. Sometimes, several arbitrators are appointed to work as a
court. Arbitration is most often used for the resolution of commercial disputes because it provides a greater
confidentiality.
Court-related mediation exists in all States, essentially in civil and commercial areas. However, only 19 states
have accredited/registered mediators and can provide their number.
It could be noted that the median number of accredited or registered mediators per 100 000 inhabitants has
strongly increased since 2014 (from 8,9 in 2014 to 19,2 in 2024). This may indicate an intent of the member States
to support the policies of enhancement of ADR through increased number of trained mediators.
The CEPEJ Study for the EU Justice Scoreboard includes for the third time data on notaries. Regarding the status
of notaries in EU, it is important to note that in 22 states notaries are holders of public offices who exercise a
public function and are appointed by the State. Thus, they are a subject of supervision by public authorities (for
instance the Ministry of Justice) and exercise their functions in a regulated environment. The number of notaries
per 100 000 inhabitants varies in EU from minimum 0,9 to maximum 27,8 with an average of 9,1 and median of 6,7
notaries per 100 000 inhabitants.
Systems of measuring and evaluating the functioning of courts and prosecution services
Most countries use quality standards for courts and public prosecution services at the national level. The number
of countries that have defined these standards exceeds half of the EU member States (15 member States).

Regarding different modalities of monitoring that are intended to review the day-to-day activity of courts through
data gathering and statistical analyses, they appear in all the EU countries. Many fields of courts activity are being
monitored particularly case flow data, courts’ decisions and efficiency indicators.
Performance and evaluation of judges and public prosecutors
As regard, individual judges and public prosecutors, it could be noted that quantitative performance targets are
defined for each judge in 8 countries, whereas 5 countries have these targets set for public prosecutors. Out of
these countries, only one doesn’t envisage sanctions if the targets are not met by judges or prosecutors (Finland),
while others have a possibility to impose different sanctions with or without disciplinary procedure, such as
warning by court president, temporary salary reduction, reflection in the individual assessment or other
sanctions. Regarding individual evaluation of the public prosecutors' work, quantitative evaluation exists in 12
member States whereas qualitative evaluation is used in 22 States.
Performance of the courts and public prosecution services
An essential element of the proper functioning of courts is the respect for the right to a fair trial within reasonable
time, as guaranteed by Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. This right must be duly considered
when analysing court workload, the length of proceedings and implementing specific measures to reduce delays
and to improve the efficiency. CEPEJ has chosen to develop efficiency court indicators at European level.
The first indicator is the Clearance Rate (CR) which indicates the capacity of the courts and judicial system to
deal with the inflow of new cases.
The second indicator is the Disposition Time (DT), that measures the theoretical time (in days) necessary for a
pending case to be solved in court in the light of the current pace of work of the courts.
When analysing the efficiency of the courts it is important to look at both indicators together and their evolution
over time.
Civil and commercial litigious cases
Looking at the CR for first instance civil and commercial litigious cases, it should be noted that almost every year
since 2014 the EU median has been equal or over 100%. The only exception is year 2020 when CR reached 98% as
the impact of COVID-19 measures affected the work of courts the most during this year. In 2024 the EU median is
97,8%, which is slightly higher compared to 97% in 2023 and is lower compared to 100,5% in 2022.
Comparing individual countries' data for 2024 and 2023, most of them (14) show decreased CRs and 9 of them
show increase which is in line with the mentioned trend. The largest decrease was registered in Italy (-15,05
percentage points) and Finland (-14,02 percent points). On the other side, 9 member States experienced
improvements of the CR with more notable increases in Estonia and Romania (with 18,5 and 13 percentage points
respectively).
To understand fully this comparison between the cycles, it is important to examine if the number of incoming and
resolved cases increased or decreased during these two years. The data shows that in 2024, the number of
incoming cases increased in 19 member States (by 4,6% in median). In some states the increase is as big as
49,9%. On the other side the number of resolved cases increased 5,6%, consequently causing the mentioned
subtle increase in CR.
As regards the Disposition Time, 13 member States increased their DT compared to 2023. More specifically, 5
countries increased it by more than 10%, 2 countries from 5-10%, 6countries from 0-5%. On the other hand, 11
countries decreased their DT, 3 of them by more than 10%, 4 between 5% and 10% and 4 by less than 5%. The
average and median numbers have not demonstrated large fluctuations but also show different tendencies. The
average DT increased by 1,9% and median DT increased by 0,4%. Generally, the situation slightly improved
because less than a half of the member states increased their DT, meaning that this cycle it might take a bit less
time to process civil and commercial litigious cases.
Administrative law cases
Compared with other categories of first instance cases in EU, administrative cases generally have highest DT of
422 days on average in 2024. For example, they still take notably longer time than the civil and commercial cases
of the first instance that need 307 days on average in 2024.
The number of countries that decreased their Disposition Time for administrative cases is 10, whereas 15
countries increased disposition time. Three countries improved their performance by decreasing the DT
significantly (more than 10%), among others, Estonia, Italy and Slovak Republic.
Increased CR is identified in 8 member States among which Slovak Republic had above +10 percent points
increase. CR decreased in 17 countries, out of which significantly (above 10 percent points) in 5, among which
Cyprus, Luxembourg, and Portugal.
This analysis shows that majority of states have demonstrated less favourable developments in 2024 regarding
administrative cases, since less than half of states have decreased their DT and increased their CR. Therefore,
more efforts will be required in future years to shorten the disposition time and come closer to DT levels of civil
and criminal cases.
Criminal law cases
Since 2020 criminal cases are reported as part of this study, without comparison with previous cycles.

Looking at the efficiency indicators for the first instance criminal cases, it is immediately notable that CR was not
very high in 2024 as EU average is 95,7% while median was 98,8%. This situation is almost identical as in 2023.
Regarding DT, in 2024 the average is 189 days and median is 128 days, whereas in 2023 the average is 175 and
median 134 days. The improvements are notable in the individual countries' DTs as 6 states reduced them.
However, 17 countries increased their level of DT some of them significantly. The maximum values were observed
in Malta (862 days) and Greece (583 days). The lowest DT was recorded in Estonia (35 days) and Hungary (51 days)
even less than last year.
The level of CR lower than 100% was reported in 18 states which might lead to backlog formation and
corresponding increase of DT in the future years. Therefore, affected states should put efforts to prevent such
negative developments. Also, countries with very high DT should continue reducing it toward average or median
EU levels in the future.
 Public prosecutors: Total number of 1st instance criminal cases
Since 2020 public prosecution’s cases are reported as part of this study, without comparison with previous
cycles.
During 2024, the average value of incoming cases by public prosecution services in the European Union was 3,24
cases per 100 inhabitants. The number of processed cases was at approximately same level (3,27). The similar
tendency was recorded for average numbers in 2023 and 2022. The identified tendency of median showed slightly
higher number for processed cases compared with incoming (3,01 for incoming and 3,08 for resolved). The
median values were also lower than average numbers probably because the average was affected by the very
large number of cases reported for some of the countries, such as Luxembourg with 10,42 incoming.
Out of processed cases, there were 2,17 discontinued cases per 100 inhabitants and 0,57 cases brought to court
(median values).
Looking at the individual countries, it is interesting to note that out of 22 that provided relevant data, 10 states
have more or equal number of processed than incoming cases, whereas in 12 states incoming outnumbered
processed cases which might potentially lead to generating backlogs in the respective prosecution services.
Comparing the ratio of processed cases vs incoming cases over the last cycle, it could be concluded that ten
countries managed to improve this ratio. Analysis of this indicator implies slight increase in efficiency of public
prosecution services in 2024.
The information and communication technology (ICT) in courts
While initially acting as a simple support tool for productivity, the information and communication technology
(ICT) becomes one of the important leverages for improvement of the efficiency of courts. The increasing role of
the ICT in improving productivity and efficiency and assisting decision making, is indeed based on the possibilities
of the automation of tasks and the inevitable general technological progress.
The questionnaire related to ICT consists of 38 questions that include deployment and usage rate of different
tools used in courts. For the needs of this study EC has selected four questions related to two different tools:
writing assistance tools and recording of court hearings.

The data show that almost all the EU member States except Cyprus have writing assistance tools, and these tools
are very present, with 95-100% deployment rate on these tools reported by 18 member States in civil and
commercial matters, 17 member States in administrative matters and 19 member States in criminal matters. This
writing assistance tool shows quite high usage rate and 12 of the countries reported 95-100% usage rate for the
civil and commercial, 11 for administrative, and 13 for criminal matter. Functionalities of the writing assistance
tools are predominantly templates, which is true for all countries, but majority also have automatically generated
text. Electronic signature, and speech to text features are present in half of the countries also. Only Hungary and
Latvia have automatic suggestion of decision for all matter while France has for civil and criminal matter.

It’s worth noting that most countries have tools for the recording of the court hearing, 18 member States have 95-
100% deployment rate, and 14 member States have 95-100% usage rate. For those that have provided
information on this tool it should be noted that deployment rate is higher for civil and for administrative matter
and slightly lower for criminal. Regarding the functionalities, for example for civil matter 22 countries use audio
recording and only 10 also video of hearings. Situation is similar for criminal but much less countries seem to
record hearings in administrative matter (18). In some countries the recording is systematic for all hearings. This
is the case in 11 countries in civil, 8 in administrative and 11 in criminal matter.
The data show that almost all the EU member States have writing assistance tools, one country did not manage to reply
to this question, while in the others these tools are very present, and 95-100% deployment rate on these tools was
reported by 18 member States in civil and commercial matters, 17 member States in administrative matters and 19
member States in criminal matters. Collection of information on usage rate is an expansion on the deployment rate
collected in previous cycles. For this tool it shows quite high usage rate and 12 of the countries reported 95-100% usage
rate for the three civil and commercial and administrative, and 13 for criminal matter. Functionalities of the writing
assistance tools are predominantly templates, which is true for all countries but quite many also have automatically
generated text, electronic signature, and speech to text features. Only Hungary and Latvia have automatic suggestion of
decision for all matter while Luxembourg has for criminal matter only.

It’s worth noting that most countries have tools for the recording of the court hearing, 16 member States have 95-100%
deployment rate, and 13 member States have 95-100% usage rate. For those that have provided information on this
tool it should be noted that deployment rate is higher for civil and for criminal matter and slightly lower for
administrative. Regarding the functionalities, for example for civil matter 20 countries use audio recording and only 8
also video of hearings. Situation is similar for criminal but much less countries seem to record hearings in administrative
matter. In some countries the recording is systematic for all hearings. This is the case in 11 countries in civil, 8 in
administrative and 11 in criminal matter.



Version française
Depuis 2012, la Commission européenne a sollicité la Commission européenne pour l’efficacité de la justice
(CEPEJ) du Conseil de l’Europe pour réaliser une étude ayant pour objet l’analyse de la situation des systèmes
judiciaires dans les Etats membres de l’UE, basée sur la méthodologie propre développée et utilisée par la CEPEJ
dans le cadre de l’évaluation du fonctionnement des systèmes judiciaires des Etats membres du Conseil de
l’Europe.
Cette étude s’appuie sur la collecte, le traitement et l’analyse des données et commentaires communiqués par
les Etats membres de l’Union Européenne (UE) au travers de :
  · données sélectionnées parmi les données collectées dans le cadre de six cycles d’évaluation (données des
  années de référence 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020 et 2022)
 · et de questionnaires spécifiques (pour les années de référence 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021 et 2023, 2024).
Cette étude sera l’une des sources utilisées par la Commission Européenne pour préparer le « Tableau de bord de
la Justice dans l’UE ».
Structure de l’étude
Conformément à la dernière proposition technique rédigée dans le cadre du contrat de contribution
JUST‑2025‑IM‑JACC/RIGH/1 – “Service to support the annual publication of the EU Justice Scoreboard ”, l’étude
porte sur les données de 2024 et leurs évolutions par rapport aux données de 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019,
2020, 2021, 2022 et 2023 Elle est divisée en deux parties :
  la première examine les systèmes judiciaires des Etats membres de l’UE à l’aide de tableaux de données par
  indicateur pour tous les Etats membres ;
  la seconde contient des fiches par pays qui présentent une analyse contextualisée pour chaque Etat membre
  de l’UE.
Principaux éléments
L’étude, au travers de 8 indicateurs, dresse un état des lieux relatif au fonctionnement du service public de la
justice sur la base des éléments sélectionnés par la Commission Européenne (CE) parmi ceux qui, d’après la
CEPEJ, sont principalement constitutifs de l’efficacité et de la qualité des systèmes judiciaires.


Ressources humaines
Plusieurs catégories de juges (professionnels, occasionnels, non professionnels) peuvent contribuer au système
judiciaire. L’étude 2024 se concentre sur les juges professionnels siégeant dans les tribunaux et la moyenne de
l’Union Européenne pour cette catégorie de juges s’élève à 22,6 juges pour 100 000 habitants (la médiane est de
23,4 juges pour 100 000 habitants). Le nombre le plus faible de juges professionnels pour 100 000 habitants est
de 3,6 et le plus élevé de 44,4. La moyenne a légèrement augmenté entre 2023 et 2024 de 21,5 à 23,4.
On peut noter que, par rapport au cycle précédent, le nombre de juges pour 100 000 habitants a augmenté de
plus de 1% dans 13 Etats membres, alors qu'il n'a diminué de plus de 1% que dans 5 pays, ce qui confirme la
tendance mentionnée de l’augmentation de la valeur médiane. Les autres pays ont fait état de variations moins
importantes, ce qui peut être interprété comme une fluctuation normale des ressources humaines au sein d'un
système.
Ce nombre dépend considérablement de l’organisation du système judiciaire et de l’existence de juges
occasionnels, de juges non professionnels ou même de Rechtspfleger.
L'existence aux côtés des juges professionnels d’un personnel compétent avec des fonctions définies et un statut
reconnu est une condition essentielle pour la qualité et l’efficacité d’un système judiciaire.
Une distinction est opérée entre cinq types de personnels non-juges :
- la fonction de "Rechtspfleger",
- le personnel non-juge dont le rôle est d’assister directement les juges,
- les personnes responsables de tâches administratives,
- le personnel technique,
- les personnels non-juges n’entrant dans aucune de ces catégories.
L'analyse des données fournies par les États membres montre des tendances différentes pour les valeurs
moyennes et médianes. Depuis 2014, le nombre moyen de personnel non-juge pour 100 000 habitants a
augmenté de 5% alors que la médiane a augmenté encore plus de 8%. Par rapport au dernier cycle, la valeur
moyenne a augmenté de 0,63 %, tandis que la valeur médiane a diminué de 1,33% . La médiane de l'Union
européenne du personnel non-juge pour 100 000 habitants est de 59,4avec un minimum de 23,9 et un maximum
de 158,8.
Il convient de noter que 12 pays ont indiqué l’existence parmi les personnels non-juge des fonctions de
"Rechspfleger " (ou équivalent).
Depuis 2020, l'étude de la CEPEJ pour le Scoreboard de l'UE inclut les services des ministères publics. La
diversité des activités des ministères publics est évidente et le nombre de procureurs pour 100 000 habitants
varie dans l'Union européenne d'un minimum de 2,9 à un maximum de 24 avec une moyenne et une médiane de
11,4 procureurs pour 100 000 habitants. Par rapport au cycle précédent, la valeur moyenne -tout comme la
médiane- ont augmenté, respectivement de 1 % et 7 %.
Les procureurs sont assistés dans leurs fonctions par du personnel non-procureur attaché aux ministères
publics. Leur nombre varie considérablement de 0,9 à 46,68 personnels non-procureurs pour 100 000 habitants
avec une moyenne de 15,5 et une médiane de 14,5. Par rapport au cycle précédent, les valeurs moyenne et
médiane sont très stables.
Concernant les salaires des juges et des procureurs, il convient de noter que leurs montants absolus varient
considérablement d'un État à l'autre, en fonction principalement de la situation économique et du niveau du PIB
par habitant. À partir de 2018, presque tous les États ont connu une tendance constante à l'augmentation des
salaires, avec 27 % de hausse du salaire annuel brut moyen des juges en début de carrière et 33 % de hausse du
salaire annuel brut moyen des juges de la Cour suprême ou de la dernière instance de recours. Une tendance
similaire est également observée pour les procureurs, avec une augmentation de 30 % du salaire annuel brut
moyen des procureurs en début de carrière et une augmentation de 36 % du salaire annuel brut moyen des
procureurs au niveau de la Cour suprême ou de la dernière instance de recours.
Dans un contexte national, les juges en début de carrière gagnent en moyenne 2 fois le salaire annuel moyen de
leur pays respectifs, alors que ce ratio est un peu plus faible pour les procureurs - 1,7. Une disparité similaire est
observée entre les juges et les procureurs auprès de la Cour suprême ou de la dernière instance de recours, où le
salaire le plus élevé d’un juge à la Cour suprême est en moyenne 4,1 fois plus important que le salaire moyen du
pays, tandis que les procureurs au même niveau gagnent 3,6 fois le salaire moyen du pays.
Avocats
Le nombre moyen d'avocats pour 100 000 habitants dans les États membres de l'UE connaît de façon générale
une tendance à la hausse depuis 2014. Entre 2014 et 2024, le nombre moyen d'avocats dans les États membres
de l'UE a augmenté de 15 % et leur nombre médian de 23 %.
Bien que les Etats du sud (tels que l'Italie, la Grèce, Chypre, l’Espagne, le Portugal etc.), mais aussi le
Luxembourg, semblent avoir un nombre plus élevé d'avocats pour 100.000 habitants, la disparité significative des
valeurs, qui se reflète également dans le ratio entre avocats et juges professionnels, suggère une hétérogénéité
considérable dans les rôles et les tâches accomplis.
Organisation judiciaire
L’étude distingue trois types de tribunaux :
-     les tribunaux de droit commun compétents dans toutes les matières pour lesquelles la compétence n’a pas
été attribuée à une juridiction spécialisée – leur dénombrement est effectué en tant qu’entités juridiques pour les
première, seconde et troisième instance ;
-     les tribunaux spécialisés de première instance et d’instances supérieures (seconde et/ou troisième instance
combinées), compris également comme entités juridiques ;
-    les tribunaux, tous niveaux confondus et de première instance, en tant qu’implantations géographiques
Depuis 2014, 12 pays ont réduit leur nombre d'implantations géographiques, 3 ont conservé le même nombre,
tandis que 11 pays ont augmenté ce nombre. Entre les deux derniers cycles, 3 pays ont augmenté et 3 pays ont
réduit le nombre d’implantations géographiques.
Le nombre d’implantations géographiques pour 100 000 habitants a diminué dans la plupart des Etats membres
(la médiane était de 1,54 tribunaux pour 100 000 habitants en 2014, 1,38 en 2016 et 1,45 en 2024, ce qui
représente une baisse de 4,5 %).
En ce qui concerne la répartition des contentieux entre entités juridiques, tous les Etats membres de l’Union
Européenne, à l’exception de la République tchèque et de la Hongrie, disposent de tribunaux de première
instance spécialisés.
Le type de tribunaux spécialisés existants le plus souvent dans les Etats Membres de l’UE sont ceux qui traitent
des affaires administratives (qui existent dans tous les pays à l’exception de cinq d’entre eux), du contentieux du
travail (existe dans 11 états membres) et des affaires commerciales (existe dans 11 états membres).
Un nombre significatif de pays dispose également d'autres tribunaux spécialisés non mentionnés (existe dans 11
états membres). Alors que la majorité des pays ont peu de types de tribunaux spécialisés, certains ont de
nombreux tribunaux spécialisés dans différentes matières comme l'Espagne et le Portugal mais aussi l'Autriche,
Chypre, la France et l'Italie.
Le Portugal, la France et Chypre ont également un grand nombre de tribunaux spécialisés de 1ère instance par
rapport à l'ensemble des tribunaux de 1ère instance (75%, 84 % et 63% respectivement). Quelques autres pays
ont également un grand nombre de tribunaux spécialisés mais ils sont inclus dans la catégorie « autre» ce qui
rend la comparaison avec les autres systèmes difficile.
Depuis 2020, les données sur les tribunaux spécialisés d’instances supérieures ont été collectées et, bien sûr,
leur nombre est inférieur à celui de la première instance. Peu de pays disposent d’un grand nombre de tribunaux
spécialisés traitant de différentes affaires au niveau des instances supérieures. Dans la plupart des autres pays
qui disposent de tribunaux spécialisés au niveau des instances supérieures, ceux-ci traitent de questions
administratives (19 pays). Il existe également des tribunaux militaires au niveau des instances supérieures. Il y a
également 4 pays qui ont des tribunaux spécialisés en première instance mais pas de tribunaux spécialisés au
niveau des instances supérieures.
Mesures alternatives au règlement des litiges (ADR - alternative dispute resolution)
Dans différents pays européens, l'utilisation des mesures alternatives au règlement des litiges (ADR) est
maintenant largement acceptée par le public et les professionnels du droit. Ces mesures contribuent à
l’amélioration de l'efficacité de la justice en fournissant aux usagers des alternatives à une procédure judiciaire
régulière.
Il existe différents types d’ADR dans les pays membres :
La médiation: il s’agit d’un procès volontaire, non contraignant de règlement des litiges privés dans lequel un tiers
impartial et indépendant aide les parties à faciliter la discussion afin de les aider à résoudre leurs difficultés et de
parvenir à un accord
La médiation conduite ou renvoyée par le tribunal : dans ce type de médiation, il y a toujours intervention d'un
juge, d’un procureur qui facilite, conseille, décide ou/et approuve la procédure.
La conciliation: le principal objectif du conciliateur est de concilier, la plupart du temps en recherchant des
concessions. Il/Elle peut proposer aux parties des suggestions pour le règlement d'un litige. Par rapport au
médiateur, le conciliateur a plus de pouvoir et il est davantage proactif.
L’arbitrage: les parties choisissent un tiers impartial - un arbitre, dont la décision définitive est contraignante. Les
parties peuvent présenter des preuves et des témoignages devant les arbitres. Parfois, il y a plusieurs arbitres
désignés qui travaillent en tant que juridiction. L'arbitrage est le plus souvent utilisé pour la résolution des litiges
commerciaux car il offre une plus grande confidentialité.
La médiation conduite ou renvoyée par le tribunal existe dans tous les Etats, essentiellement en matière civile ou
commerciale. Toutefois, seuls 19 États ont des médiateurs accrédités/enregistrés et peuvent fournir leur nombre.
Il convient de noter que la médiane du nombre de médiateurs agréés ou enregistrés pour 100 000 habitants a
fortement augmenté depuis 2014 (de 8,9 en 2014 à 19,2 en 2024). Cela peut indiquer une intention des États
membres de soutenir les politiques de renforcement des ADR par l'augmentation du nombre de médiateurs
formés.
L'étude de la CEPEJ pour le tableau de bord de la justice de l'UE inclut pour la troisième fois des données sur les
notaires. En ce qui concerne le statut des notaires dans l'UE, il est important de noter que dans 22 Etats, les
notaires sont des titulaires de charges publiques qui exercent une fonction publique et sont nommés par l'Etat.
Ils sont donc soumis au contrôle des autorités publiques (par exemple le ministère de la justice) et exercent leurs
fonctions dans un environnement réglementé. Le nombre de notaires pour 100 000 habitants varie dans l'Union
Européenne entre un minimum de 0,9 et un maximum de 27,8 avec une moyenne de 9,1 et une valeur médiane de
6,7 notaires pour 100 000 habitants.

Système pour mesurer et évaluer le fonctionnement des tribunaux et des services des ministères publics
La plupart des pays utilisent des normes de qualité au niveau national dans les tribunaux et les services des
ministères publics. Le nombre de pays ayant défini ces normes est supérieur à la moitié des Etats membres de
l'UE (15 États membres).
En ce qui concerne les différentes modalités de suivi destinées à examiner l'activité quotidienne des tribunaux
par le biais de la collecte de données et d'analyses statistiques, elles existent dans tous les pays de l'UE. De
nombreux domaines de l'activité des tribunaux font l'objet d'un suivi, en particulier les données sur les flux
d'affaires, les décisions des tribunaux et les indicateurs d'efficacité.
Performance et évaluation des juges et des procureurs

Concernant les juges et les procureurs individuellement, on peut noter que des objectifs quantitatifs de
performance sont définis pour chaque juge dans 8 pays, tandis que 5 pays fixent ces objectifs pour les
procureurs. Parmi ces pays, un seul, la Finlande, n’envisage pas de sanctions si les objectifs ne sont pas atteints
par les juges ou les procureurs, tandis que les autres ont la possibilité d'imposer différentes sanctions avec ou
sans procédure disciplinaire, telles que l'avertissement par le président du tribunal, la réduction temporaire du
salaire, la prise en compte dans l'évaluation individuelle ou d'autres sanctions.
En ce qui concerne l'évaluation individuelle du travail des procureurs, l'évaluation quantitative existe dans 12
pays, tandis que l'évaluation qualitative est utilisée dans 22 États.
Performance des tribunaux et services du ministère public
Un élément essentiel du bon fonctionnement des tribunaux est le respect du droit à un procès équitable dans un
délai raisonnable, tel que garanti par l'article 6 de la Convention européenne des droits de l'homme. Ce droit doit
être dûment pris en compte lors de l'analyse de la charge de travail des tribunaux, de la durée des procédures et
de la mise en œuvre de mesures spécifiques pour réduire les délais et améliorer l'efficacité. La CEPEJ a choisi de
développer des indicateurs d'efficacité des tribunaux au niveau européen.
Le premier indicateur est le taux de variation du stock d'affaires pendantes (Clearance Rate-CR) qui montre la
capacité du tribunal et du système judiciaire à faire face au flux d’affaires nouvelles.
Le second indicateur est la durée estimée d'écoulement du stock, qui mesure le temps théorique (en jours)
nécessaire pour qu'une affaire pendante soit résolue par un tribunal, compte tenu du rythme de travail actuel des
tribunaux.
Lorsque l'on analyse l'efficacité des tribunaux, il est important d'examiner les deux indicateurs ensemble et leur
évolution dans le temps.
Affaires civiles et commerciales contentieuses
Si l'on examine le Clearance rate (CR) des affaires civiles et commerciales de première instance, il convient de
noter que la médiane de l'UE est égale ou supérieure à 100 % presque chaque année depuis 2014. La seule
exception est l'année 2020, où le CR a atteint 98 %, car c'est au cours de cette année que l'impact des mesures
COVID-19 a le plus affecté le travail des tribunaux. En 2024, la médiane de l'UE est de 97,8%, ce qui est
légèrement plus élevé par rapport à 97 % en 2023 et est inférieur par rapport à 100,5 % en 2022.

Si l'on compare les données des différents pays pour 2024 et 2023, la plupart d'entre eux (14) affichent des
diminutions des CR et 9 d’entre eux montrent une hausse des CR, ce qui correspond à la tendance mentionnée.
Les plus fortes diminutions étant enregistrées en Italie (-15,05 points de pourcentage) et en Finlande (-14,02
points de pourcentage). Neuf pays connaissent par ailleurs une amélioration de leur CR, avec une augmentation
plus notable en l’Estonie et à la Roumanie (avec 18,5 et 13points de pourcentage respectivement).

Pour mieux comprendre cette comparaison entre les cycles, il convient d’examiner si le nombre d'affaires
nouvelles et terminées a augmenté ou diminué au cours de ces deux années. Les données montrent qu’en 2024,
le nombre d’affaires nouvelles a augmenté dans 19 Etats membres (avec une médiane de 4,6%). Dans certains
États, l'augmentation atteint même 49,9 %. En revanche, le nombre d’affaires terminées a augmenté de 5,6 %, ce
qui a entraîné une légère augmentation du CR mentionnée précédemment.
En ce qui concerne le Disposition Time (DT), 13 États membres ont vu leur DT augmenter par rapport à 2023. Plus
précisément, 5 pays ont connu une augmentation de plus de 10%, 2 pays de 5 à 10%, 6 pays de 0 à 5%. Par
ailleurs, 11 pays ont vu leur DT diminuer, 3 de plus de 10 %, 4 entre 5% et 10% et 4 de moins de 5%. Les valeurs
moyennes et médianes n'ont pas connu de grandes fluctuations, mais montrent également des tendances
différentes. Le DT moyen a augmenté de 1,9% et le DT médian a augmenté de 0,4 %. D'une manière générale, la
situation s'est légèrement améliorée car moins de la moitié des États membres ont augmenté leur DT, ce qui
signifie que le traitement des affaires civiles et commerciales pourrait prendre un peu moins de temps au cours
de ce cycle.
Affaires de droit administratif
Par rapport aux autres catégories d'affaires de première instance au sein de l'UE, les affaires administratives
présentent en général le DT le plus élevé, soit 422 jours en moyenne en 2024. Elles sont par exemple nettement
plus longues que les affaires civiles et commerciales de première instance, qui nécessitent 307 jours en moyenne
en 2024.
Le nombre de pays qui ont diminué leur DT pour les affaires administratives est de 10, tandis que 15 pays ont
augmenté ce DT. Trois pays ont amélioré leurs performances en diminuant le DT de manière significative (plus de
10%), parmi lesquels l’Estonie, l’Italie et la République slovaque.
L'augmentation du Clearance Rate peut être identifiée dans 8 pays parmi lesquels la République slovaque qui ont
enregistré une augmentation de plus de +10 points de pourcentage.
Le Clearance Rate a diminué dans 17 pays, et de manière significative (plus de 10 points de pourcentage) dans 5
d’entre eux, dont Chypre, le Luxembourg et le Portugal.
Cette analyse montre que la majorité des États ont évolué moins favorablement en 2024 en ce qui concerne les
affaires administratives, puisque moins de la moitié d'entre eux ont diminué leur DT et augmenté leur CR. Par
conséquent, des efforts supplémentaires seront nécessaires dans les années à venir pour réduire les DT et se
rapprocher des niveaux des DT des affaires civiles et pénales.
Affaires de droit pénal
Depuis 2020, les affaires pénales sont incluses dans cette étude, sans comparaison avec les cycles précédents.
Si l'on examine les indicateurs d'efficacité pour les affaires pénales de première instance, on remarque d'emblée
que le CR n'était pas très élevé en 2024, la moyenne de l'UE étant de 95,7 % tandis que la médiane se situait à
98,8 %. La situation est quasiment identique à celle de 2023.
En ce qui concerne le DT, en 2024 la moyenne est de 189 jours et la médiane de 128 jours, alors qu'en 2023 la
moyenne est de 175 jours et la médiane de 134 jours. Les améliorations ne sont notables que pour les DT des
différents pays, puisque 6 États les ont réduits. Cependant, 17 pays ont augmenté leur niveau de DT, dont
certains de manière significative. Les valeurs maximales ont été observées à Malte (862 jours) et en Grèce (583
jours). Le DT le plus bas a été enregistré en Estonie (35 jours) et en Hongrie (51 jours), soit encore moins que
l'année dernière.
Un niveau de CR inférieur à 100 % a été signalé dans les 18 États, ce qui pourrait entraîner la création d'arriérés et
une augmentation correspondante du DT dans les années à venir. Par conséquent, les États concernés doivent
s'efforcer de prévenir de telles évolutions négatives. De même, les pays présentant un niveau de DT très élevé
doivent continuer à le réduire pour atteindre les niveaux moyens ou médians de l'UE dans les années à venir.
Procureurs publics : Nombre total d'affaires pénales de première instance
Depuis 2020, les affaires du ministère public sont incluses dans cette étude, sans comparaison avec les cycles
précédents. En 2024, la valeur moyenne des affaires nouvelles reçues par les services du ministère public dans
l'Union européenne était de 3,24 affaires pour 100 habitants. Le nombre d'affaires traitées se situait
approximativement au même niveau (3,27). La même tendance a été enregistrée pour les valeurs moyennes en
2023 et 2022. Les valeurs médiane montrent un nombre légèrement plus élevé d’affaires traitées que d’affaires
nouvelles (3,01 pour les affaires nouvelles et 3,08 pour les affaires traitées). Si ces valeurs médianes étaient
également inférieures aux nombres moyens, c’est aussi probablement parce que la moyenne était affectée par le
très grand nombre d’affaires indiqués pour certains pays, tels que le Luxembourg avec 10,42 affaires nouvelles.
Parmi les affaires traitées, il y a eu 2,17 affaires classées pour 100 habitants (valeur médiane) et 0,57 affaire
portée devant le tribunal (valeur médiane).
Si l'on considère les pays individuellement, il est intéressant de noter que sur les 22 qui ont fourni des données
pertinentes, 10 Etats ont plus d'affaires traitées que d'affaires nouvelles ou un nombre égal pour ces deux
catégories, tandis que dans 12 Etats, les affaires nouvelles étaient plus nombreuses que les affaires traitées, ce
qui pourrait potentiellement conduire à la création d'arriérés dans les services de poursuite respectifs. La
comparaison du ratio entre affaires traitées et affaires nouvelles au cours du dernier cycle permet de conclure
que dix pays ont réussi à améliorer ce ratio. L'analyse de cet indicateur suggère une légère augmentation de
l'efficacité des services du ministère public en 2024.
L’utilisation des technologies de l’information et de la communication (TIC) dans les tribunaux
Alors qu'elles agissaient initialement comme un simple outil de soutien à la productivité, les technologies de
l'information et de la communication (TIC) deviennent l'un des leviers importants pour améliorer l’efficacité des
tribunaux. Le rôle croissant des TIC dans l’amélioration de la productivité et de l'efficacité, ainsi que dans l'aide à
la prise de décision, repose en effet sur les possibilités de l'automatisation des tâches et l'inévitable progrès
technologique général.
Le questionnaire relatif aux TIC comprend 38 questions qui incluent le taux de déploiement et le taux d'utilisation
des différents outils utilisés dans les tribunaux. Pour les besoins de cette étude, la Commission européenne a
sélectionné quatre questions relatives à deux outils différents : les outils d'assistance à la rédaction et
l'enregistrement des audiences.
Les données montrent que presque tous les pays de l'UE sauf Chypre disposent d'outils d’assistance à la
rédaction, et ces outils sont très présents avec un taux de déploiement de 95-100% indiqué par 18 Etats
membres pour le domaine civil et commercial, 17 pour le domaine administratif et 19 pour le domaine pénal.
Pour cet outil d’assistance à la rédaction, le taux d'utilisation est assez élevé : 12 des pays ont déclaré un taux
d'utilisation de 95 - 100 % pour le domaine civil et commercial et 11 pour le domaine administratif, 13 pour le
domaine pénal. Les fonctionnalités des outils d'aide à la rédaction sont principalement des modèles, ce qui est
vrai pour tous les pays, mais un grand nombre d'entre eux disposent également de textes générés
automatiquement. La signature électronique et de la conversion automatique de la voix en texte (transcription
automatique) sont également présentes dans la moitié des pays. Seule la Hongrie et la Lettonie disposent de
décision de justice proposée automatiquement pour toutes les affaires, tandis que la France en dispose pour les
affaires civiles et pénales.
Il convient de noter que la plupart des pays disposent d’outils d’enregistrement des audiences, 18 États membres
ont un taux de déploiement de 95 à 100 % et 14 États membres ont un taux d'utilisation de 95 - 100 %. Pour ceux
qui ont fourni des informations sur cet outil, il est notable que le taux de déploiement est plus élevé pour le
domaine civil et administratif et légèrement inférieur pour le domaine pénal. En ce qui concerne les
fonctionnalités, pour les affaires civiles, 22 pays utilisent l'enregistrement audio et seulement 10 l'enregistrement
vidéo des audiences. La situation est similaire en matière pénale, mais beaucoup moins de pays semblent
enregistrer les audiences en matière administrative (18). Dans certains pays, l'enregistrement est systématique
pour toutes les audiences. C'est le cas dans 11 pays en matière civile, 8 en matière administrative et 11 en
matière pénale.

Les questions relatives aux TIC ont été complètement remaniées en 2022 et consistent en 38 questions qui incluent le
taux de déploiement et le taux d'utilisation des différents outils utilisés dans les tribunaux. Pour les besoins de cette
étude, la Commission européenne a sélectionné quatre questions relatives à deux outils différents : les outils
d'assistance à la rédaction et l'enregistrement des audiences.


Les données montrent que presque tous les pays de l'UE disposent d'outils d’assistance à la rédaction, un pays n'a pas
pu répondre à cette question, alors que dans les autres pays, ces outils sont très présents et un taux de déploiement de
95-100% de ces outils a été reporté dans 18 Etats membres pour le domaine civil et commercial, 17 Etats membres
pour le domaine administratif et 19 Etats membres pour le domaine pénal. Les informations collectées sur le taux
d'utilisation sont une extension de celles concernant le taux de déploiement collectées pour les cycles précédents. Pour
cet outil, le taux d'utilisation est assez élevé : 12 % des pays ont déclaré un taux d'utilisation de 95 à 100 % pour les
affaires civiles et commerciales et les affaires administratives, 13 pour les affaires pénales. Les fonctionnalités des outils
d'aide à la rédaction sont principalement des modèles, ce qui est vrai pour tous les pays, mais un grand nombre d'entre
eux disposent également de textes générés automatiquement, de la signature électronique et de la conversion
automatique de la voix en texte. Seule la Hongrie et la Lettonie disposent de décision de justice proposée
automatiquement pour toutes les affaires, tandis que le Luxembourg ne le fait que pour les affaires pénales.


Il convient de noter que la plupart des pays disposent d’outils d’enregistrement des audiences, 16 États membres ont
un taux de déploiement de 95 à 100 % et 13 États membres ont un taux d'utilisation de 95 à 100 %. Pour ceux qui ont
fourni des informations sur cet outil, il est notable que le taux de déploiement est plus élevé pour les affaires civiles et
pénales et légèrement inférieur pour les affaires administratives. En ce qui concerne les fonctionnalités, pour les affaires
civiles, 20 pays utilisent l'enregistrement audio et seulement 8 l'enregistrement vidéo des audiences. La situation est
similaire en matière pénale, mais beaucoup moins de pays semblent enregistrer les audiences en matière
administrative. Dans certains pays, l'enregistrement est systématique pour toutes les audiences. C'est le cas dans 11
pays en matière civile, 8 en matière administrative et 11 en matière pénale.
CEPEJ(2025)21rev - Part 1
            Methodology
            The methodology used for this study completely follows CEPEJ methodology for its evaluation cycle
            using a questionnaire for evaluating European judicial systems. This Scheme is filled by the
            CEPEJ’s national correspondents, whose responses are statistically processed and analysed by the
            Secretariat of the CEPEJ.
            Such inter-governmental work requires permanent dialogue and full transparency with the member
            states of the Council of Europe.

            •   Data collection, validation and analysis
            Numbers indicated between brackets following the letter Q refer to the questions of the CEPEJ
            questionnaire.
            From a methodological point of view, and with a commitment to quality, consistency and
            comparability of the data supplied, data collection is primarily responsibility of the CEPEJ’s national
            correspondents. The national correspondents are the unique interlocutors of the Secretariat when
            collecting new data. States providing such data are liable for the quality of data used in the survey.
            According to CEPEJ methodology, an extensive work is carried out by the CEPEJ Secretariat to
            verify the quality of the data submitted by the correspondents. This quality check process requires a
            certain time in order to guarantee the reliability of the quantitative and qualitative data to be finally
            presented to European Commission.
            The reference year for the last data collection is 2024. As for previous cycles, wherever data is not
            possible to obtain notation NA (not available) is used. Only in exceptional cases and only for
            questions that are used for standardisation, CEPEJ can accept previous cycle data. This data is
            population, GDP per capita and average annual salary.
            The study itself is based on 2024 data as well on previous cycles (every year, starting with 2014)
            wherever evolution and trends are presented. "


            •   The quality of data

            The reader should bear in mind and always interpret statistical figures presented (including in the
            country fiches) in the light of their attached narrative comments which allow to contextualise the
            data and give more information on each specific judicial system.


            The CEPEJ has chosen to process and present only the data which offered a high level of quality
            and accountability: it decided to disregard figures which were too different from one country to
            another or from one exercise to another without sufficient explanations, or when they did not
            present sufficient guarantees of reliability. For some issues covered by this study, no data could be
            provided. This could mean that none were available, that the data could not be collected as such or
            that no data meeting these requirements had been provided within the deadline set.


            •   The following abbreviations have been used in this study:
            NA: data not available;
            NAP: data non applicable;
            CR: Clearance Rate;
            DT: Disposition Time.

            Methodological disclaimer

            1) The data analysed have been provided by the member states and/or have then been validated
            during quality control process finalised 15th December 2025. Amendments provided by member
            states after the delivery of this study may appear in future reports, as CEPEJ’s database is regularly
            updated. This also explains why previous cycle data updated on the day of this delivery, may not
            always fully coincide with the data published in previous CEPEJ reports and studies (even
            sometimes replacing data with “NA”).

            The validation has been made according to CEPEJ’s methodology. However, the full reliability of
            data depends mostly on the data providers. It should be kept in mind that the accuracy of some
            entries was confirmed by national correspondents without specific explanation on potential
            discrepancies.

            2) Some data cannot be compared with previous data since the questionnaire was modified
            between the different evaluation cycles, this is signalised in comments or footnotes under the
            concerned tables.

            3) It should also be noted that the minimum, maximum, average and median values in certain
            tables are calculated with quantified data (excluding answers “NA” or “NAP”).
            4) Certain indicators as well as variations might appear as outliers only because of small absolute
            numbers. This could be the case of small countries, In this case the indicator or variation is not
            considered as relevant.
            5) The CEPEJ works in full transparency vis-à-vis the member states as regards the purpose of the
            data collection exercise. According to CEPEJ methodology, only the final version of the study can
            be disseminated, after possible comments from the member states. Before the final version of the
            study, all the data collected remains confidential. When using data provided by the CEPEJ in public
            reports, European Commission should always mention “Source: CEPEJ data”. If CEPEJ data are
            presented together with other data, the source of the different data must be clearly mentioned.

            6) Certain indicators as well as variations might apear as outliers only because of small absolute
            numbers. This could be the case of small countries, In this case the indicator or variation is not
            considered as relevant.
            7) The analyses delivered in the country profiles are based on the data and comments provided
            from the CEPEJ national correspondent and without use of additional sources.

     Q004 (General Comment): Average gross annual salary is based on provisional numbers, definitive numbers (usually
     available in the next year) may differ slightly from those provided here.
     Salary is defined as 'reward per working year'. This reward consists of salary (gross salary, including taxes and social
     contributions/premiums), rewards like holiday stipends, payment in kind, expense allowances tied in with work (e.g. travel
     allowances), and social premiums for the employer (payments for lawful and contractual social security, like pension
     contributions). The CBS has somewhat different numbers available than those used by Eurostat, therefore, numbers presented
     here might differ from those in Eurostat.
     Q004 (2020): These are provisional numbers and the definitive numbers (available in 2022) may differ slightly from these
     provided here. The data specifies ‘reward per working year’ as salary. The reward consists of salary (gross salary, as it
     includes taxes and social contributions/premiums), rewards like holiday stipends, payment in kind, expense allowances that tie
     in with work (like travel allowances that cover costs to and from work), and social premiums that are for the employer
     (payments for lawful and contractual social security, like pension contributions).

     Q004 (2019): The Statistics Bureau only had numbers for 2018. 2019 data was not available at the moment of data collection.

     Q004 (2018): This is average salary of all employees; the number includes money that employers pay for pension plans, social
     security (money that is paid directly to employees). The statistic does not include the income of people who are not employees
     (people without work, employers).
     Q004 (2016): Compared to previous questionaires (before 2014) these figures have been adjusted according to new rules of
     the european system of national accounts (illegal activities are now included)

     (19638309 -as communicated in September 2017).
     Update:
     After reviewing/completing of population data by the National Institute of Statistics, in accordance with the methodology of
     calculation, the revised data are as follows- for January 1, 2015, the number of inhabitants (as revised) is 19875542; for
     January 1, 2016, the number of inhabitants (final data) is 19760314; for January 1, 2017, the number of inhabitants (final data)
     is 19644350.
     Methodological explanations:
     Reference moments for statistically determining the usual resident population are January 1st and July 1st, t year. The data on
     usual resident population at the moment of January 1st, t year are available on August (provisional data) and on January, t+1
     year (final data). Usual resident population represents all persons of Romanian nationality, foreign or stateless who have their
     usual residence in Romania. Usual residence is the place where a person normally spends the daily period of rest, regardless
     of temporary absences for purposes of recreation, holidays, visits to friends and relatives, business, medical treatment or
     religious pilgrimage. The usual residence may be the same as the domicile or may differ from it, for the persons who choose to
     establish their usual residence in a locality other than the locality of domicile in the country or abroad. It is considered having
     their usual residence in a specific geographic area just people who have lived in that usual residence for a continuous period
     of at least 12 months prior to reference moment. The resident population includes the persons who immigrated to Romania but
     excludes the persons who emigrated from Romania. In order to carry out international comparisons, it will be used only the
     usual resident population, calculated according to European regulations (Regulation no. 1260/2013 of the European
     Parliament and of the Council on European demographic statistics and Regulation no. 205/2014 laying down uniformed
     conditions for the implementation of Regulation no. 1260/2013 on European demographic statistics as regards breakdowns of
     data, deadlines and data revisions). For the period between the last two censuses (2002-2011 period), data refers to usual
     resident population, re-estimated under comparability conditions with final results of the Population and Housing Census of
     2011. After January 1st, 2012, the usual resident population on January 1st was estimated according to the usual residence
     criterion, using the components method.
     The revised data are available in the TEMPO database of the National Institute of Statistics (www.insse.ro).

     Q072 (2024): Judicial proceedings – of both courts and public prosecution services – are systematically monitored for undue
     waiting periods. Depending on the type of proceeding a waiting period (= time during which no steps are taken in the
     proceeding) of three months, six months or twelve months is considered to be potentially undue. A waiting period exceeding
     this timeframe will lead to the proceeding appearing on an automatically generated list for review. The answer is different from
     last years, because the question has not been answered correctly in the past.

     Q072 (2016): Supreme administrative Court: Statistic of incoming cases, number of decisions delivered, number of postpones
     cases, length of proceedings (timeframes) and age of cases
     Q083 (2018): There are no specific targets given to the Judges, which are seen as a conflict with the Independence of Courts.

     Q083 (2016): Provincial Administrative Courts: Maximum 150 cases a year per judge (average value).
     Federal Finance Court:
     No performance targets, which are seen in conflict with the independence. However based on a continuous transparent
     controlling the possibility of benchmarking exists. In addition regular dialogues with the judges regarding their performance are
     held.

CEPEJ study on the functioning of judicial systems
in the EU Member States                                                                                                          50 / 1444
     Q083-1 (General Comment): No specific targets are formulated in respect of judges.
     Q083-1 (2016): Answer counts only for the administrative courts.
     For the other courts, no performance targets, which are seen as a conflict with the independence of courts.
     Q083-3 (2018): There are no specific targets given to public prosecutors.
     Q120 (General Comment): In the Austrian judicial system we have diverse and multifaceted statistic products, which are an
     important basis for the management of justice. The statistics are regularly compiled by the Federal Computing Center and
     serve to control the deployment of personnel, but also for the supervision that is necessarily linked to the parties' right to a fair
     trial. The work of the public prosecutors is continuously and systematically reviewed on a quantitative level (i.e. number of
     completed cases, duration of proceedings). In this way, major deviations from the average can be identified. If a public
     prosecutor shows too many delays in proceedings or excessively long proceedings, this can lead to disciplinary proceedings or
     even a reduction in their job description. The assessment is carried out by the heads of the senior public prosecutors' offices. A
     qualitative assessment of each prosecutor’s work is carried out once for the second calendar year following their appointment
     to a specific position. The evaluation is repeated when they are appointed to a new position (for the second calendar year
     following that appointment). An assessment at a later time will be carried out, if either the head of the prosecutor’s office or the
     assessed prosecutor themselves have reason to believe that the result of the last assessment is no longer accurate. If the
     assessment finds the prosecutor’s work to be below average, the assessment is repeated for the next calendar year. The
     assessment is carried out by the personnel commission at the Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office, consisting of the Head of the
     Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Head Prosecutor for the Public Prosecutor’s Office to which the assessed prosecutor
     belongs, one prosecutor appointed/chosen by the Union of Public Services and one prosecutor appointed/chosen by staff
     representatives.
     The evaluation takes into account the prosecutor’s professional abilities, skills, knowledge, conduct and performance. The
     assessment can be relevant for the prosecutor’s career, as it will be taken into account in later application procedures. If the
     assessment finds the prosecutor’s work failing to meet the absolute minimum peformance standards necessary to fulfill their
     duties for two consecutive calendar years, the prosecutor will be dismissed.




     Q120 (2024): In the Austrian judicial system we have diverse and multifaceted statistic products, which are an important basis
     for the management of justice. The statistics are regularly compiled by the Federal Computing Center and serve to control the
     deployment of personnel, but also for the supervision that is necessarily linked to the parties' right to a fair trial. The work of the
     public prosecutors is continuously and systematically reviewed on a quantitative level (i.e. number of completed cases,
     duration of proceedings). In this way, major deviations from the average can be identified. If a public prosecutor shows too
     many delays in proceedings or excessively long proceedings, this can lead to disciplinary proceedings or even a reduction in
     their job description. The assessment is carried out by the heads of the senior public prosecutors' offices. A qualitative
     assessment of each prosecutor’s work is carried out once for the second calendar year following their appointment to a
     specific position. The evaluation is repeated when they are appointed to a new position (for the second calendar year following
     that appointment). An assessment at a later time will be carried out, if either the head of the prosecutor’s office or the
     assessed prosecutor themselves have reason to believe that the result of the last assessment is no longer accurate. If the
     assessment finds the prosecutor’s work to be below average, the assessment is repeated for the next calendar year. The
     assessment is carried out by the personnel commission at the Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office, consisting of the Head of the
     Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Head Prosecutor for the Public Prosecutor’s Office to which the assessed prosecutor
     belongs, one prosecutor appointed/chosen by the Union of Public Services and one prosecutor appointed/chosen by staff
     representatives.
     The evaluation takes into account the prosecutor’s professional abilities, skills, knowledge, conduct and performance. The
     assessment can be relevant for the prosecutor’s career, as it will be taken into account in later application procedures. If the
     assessment finds the prosecutor’s work failing to meet the absolute minimum peformance standards necessary to fulfill their
     duties for two consecutive calendar years, the prosecutor will be dismissed.

     Q120 (General Comment): Public prosecutors are assessed on the way in which they carry out their duties. Heads of
     divisions are also assessed on their management skills and staff management, as well as on initiatives taken to tackle the
     backlog of cases. The criteria on which this assessment is based are of 3 types:
     1) legal knowledge, work efficiency and effectiveness, communication, decisiveness and professional ethics
     2) collegiality and self-control
     3) interest in continuous training, adaptability and open-mindedness, commitment.
     The purpose of the assessment is to ensure quality control, but also to provide a form of coaching that contributes to the
     prosecutor’s development and to anticipate difficulties or a possible negative mention.
     Assessment also plays an essential role in consideration for a subsequent appointment or designation.
     Competent authorities:
     The assessment is carried out by an absolute majority of votes cast by the head of division and two prosecutors appointed by
     the general assembly or by the division assembly.
     The assessment of the heads of divisions is carried out by the competent chamber of the assessment board, which is made up
     of two heads of divisions from the public prosecutor's office, two magistrates who are members of the Opinion and
     Investigation Commission of the High Council of the Judiciary, a magistrate of the Court of Audit and a human resources
     management specialist (see articles 259novies et seq. of the Judicial Code).

     Q066 (2020): Judiciary system Act:
     Article. 198 (1) The criteria for the appraisal of a judge, prosecutor or an investigating magistrate shall be:
     1. legal knowledge and skills of applying it;
     2. skill of analysing legally relevant facts;
     3. skill of making optimum working arrangements;
     4. efficiency and discipline;
     5. compliance with the rules of ethical behaviour.
     (2) In the course of the appraisal under Paragraph (1) the following indicators shall be taken into account:
     1. keeping deadlines;
     2. number of instruments upheld and reversed and the grounds for this;
     3. the results of inspections carried out by the Inspectorate with the Supreme Judicial Council,
     4. the overall caseload of the respective judicial district and judicial authority, as well as the workload of the appraised judge,
     prosecutor or investigating magistrate compared to other judges, prosecutors or investigating magistrates in the same judicial
     authority.
     (4) The time served by the judge, prosecutor or investigating magistrate as a permanent trainer at the National Institute of
     Justice shall also be included in the appraisal period. The evaluation of the work performance as a trainer shall be given by the
     Managing Board.
     (5) The time served by the judge, prosecutor or investigating magistrate as an European Delegated Prosecutor shall also be
     included in the appraisal period. The evaluation of the results of their work under Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 shall become part
     of their appraisal.
     Article. 199. (1) A judge shall be appraised under the following specific criteria:
     1. complying with the schedule for conduct of court hearings;
     2. skill of conducting a court hearing and drawing up a record of proceedings;
     3. administrating cases and appeals, preparing for a court hearing;
     4. number of appealed judicial instruments from among the appealable judicial instruments, appealed judicial instruments
     upheld, judicial instruments reversed or invalidated, in whole or in part, and the grounds for it; the ability to reason and justify
     judicial instruments and to analyse evidence shall be subject to evaluation.
     (2) A prosecutor shall be appraised under the following specific criteria:
     1. skills of planning and structuring steps in pre-trial and trial proceedings;
     2. complying with the written instructions and orders of the superior prosecutor;

     Q072 (2024): The Inspectorate to the Supreme Judicial Council (ISJC):
     One of the main powers of the Inspectorate to the Supreme Judicial Council (ISJC) is to "check the organization of the
     initiation and progress of court, prosecution, and investigation cases, as well as the completion of cases within the established
     time limits" (Article 54, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Judiciary System Act). In exercising this power, the ISJC monitors for delays
     in the course of the relevant proceedings, which is done within the framework of the inspections carried out on the judicial
     authorities (comprehensive planned/scheduled inspections or inspections based on reports/signals) or when conducting
     preliminary investigations into reports/signals from individuals or legal entities of violations in the handling of cases. This year,
     the ISJC is responding to the questionnaire for the first time, as it has not been sent to it before. In previous years, the SJC
     probably gave a negative answer to this question in view of its own powers, rather than those exercised by the ISJC, which is
     an independent body separate from the SJC.

     Prosecutоr's Office of RB: Such a system exists. According to Art. 196 of the Judicial System Act the evaluation is carried out
     in advance, in order to acquire irreplaceability, periodic and extraordinary attestation of the magistrates, and the criteria for the
     same are defined in Art. 198 of the Judicial System Act: legal knowledge and skills; ability to analyze legally relevant facts;
     ability to optimally organize work; expediency and discipline; compliance with the rules of ethical conduct. Attestation also
     takes into account the following indicators: compliance with deadlines; number of confirmed and canceled acts and the
     reasons for this; the results of the inspections of the Inspectorate at the Supreme Judicial Council; the overall workload of the
     relevant judicial authority, as well as the workload of the assessed judge, prosecutor or investigator compared to other judges,
     prosecutors or investigators from the same judicial authority.




     Q120-1 (General Comment): Quantitative evaluation of the work of the prosecutors is carried out by applying the Rules for
     measuring the workload of the prosecutor's offices and the individual workload of each prosecutor and investigator, adopted by
     the Prosecution College/collegium of the SJC. It is possible to display the data according to the indicators provided for in the
     Rules in real time, both for the prosecutor's office as a whole, as well as for individual prosecutor's offices and for each specific
     prosecutor.
     Quantitative data on the workload are taken into account in the appraisal procedure of a specific prosecutor, in the course of
     which an assessment of his work is carried out, both in terms of quantitative indicators and also regarding the quality of the
     performed activity according to the results achieved.
     Prosecutors are assessed in accordance with Ordinance No. 3 of February 23, 2017 of the Supreme Judicial Council on the
     indicators and Methodology for Assessment and the Criteria for Reporting the Workload Degree of Prosecutors and
     Investigators and of Administrative Heads and Their Deputies (promulgated SG No. 21 /10.03.2017).
     Attestation is carried out:
     1. in advance - for a three-year period from the appointment to the position of prosecutor or investigator - when participating in
     a competition or when being offered a promotion;
     2. to acquire irreplaceability - upon completion of 5 years of experience as a prosecutor or investigator;
     3. periodically - for a 5-year period from the attestation of irreplaceability of a prosecutor and investigator, of an administrative
     head and of a deputy administrative head;
     4. extraordinary - in the cases under Art. 197, para. 5 of the Judicial System Act.
     Junior prosecutors and junior investigators are not assessed in advance, and a report on their work is prepared by the mentor
     in the second year of their appointment.
