     Bulgaria
     Q070-1 (General Comment): .Other: The Inspectorate to the Supreme Judicial Council, pursuant to Art. 54 of the Judiciary
     System Act, examines the organization of the administrative duties of the courts, prosecutor's offices and investigative bodies;
     reviews the organization of the initiation and motions of court, prosecutor's and investigative proceedings, as well as the
     closure of cases within the established deadlines; analyzes and summarizes the cases that have been closed by a final court
     act, as well as the closed files and cases of prosecutors and investigators, adopting a procedure for regular reporting and
     publication of the results of the analysis and summary of the closed cases; in the event of contradictory judiciary practices,
     observed in the execution of work pursuant to Article 54(1)(3) of the Judiciary System Act, notifies the respective authorities to
     request the adoption of interpretative decisions or interpretative rulings; performs integrity and conflict of interest checks for
     judges, prosecutors and investigators on their property declarations, as well as on the detection of actions that violate the
     reputation of the judiciary and those related to the breach of the independence of judges, prosecutors and investigators;
     reviews applications against the hearing and settlement of cases within a reasonable timeline, prepares an annual programme
     for planned inspections and an annual report on its activities, submitted to the Plenum of the Supreme Judicial Council; adopts
     a model for reporting on the settlement of cases within the legal timeline in the performance of duties under Article 54, (1)(2) of
     the Judiciary System Act, in coordination with the Supreme Judicial Council; prepares annual summaries of good and bad
     practices in terms of compliance with the ethical rules in accordance with the relevant European and international standards in
     relation to the abovementioned checks and provides the information to the relevant Colleges of the Supreme Judicial Council.




     Q070-1 (2024): Pursuant to Art. 54 of the JSA The Inspectorate with the Supreme Judicial Council (ISJC) shall check the
     organization of administrative operation of the courts, prosecution offices and investigating authorities; check the
     arrangements made for the institution and progress of court, prosecutorial and investigative cases, as well as the disposal
     thereof within the established time limits; analyze and summarize the cases that have been closed by an effective judicial act,
     as well as the closed files and cases of prosecutors and investigators, by adopting a procedure for regular reporting and
     publishing of the results of the analysis and summarizing the closed cases; in the presence of conflicting case-law, the
     existence of which has been found in carrying out the activity under Art. 54 (1), item 3 of the JSA, it shall alert the competent
     authorities of the need to request the rendition of interpretative judgements or interpretative decrees; carry out integrity testing
     and examinations for conflict of interest of judges, prosecutors and investigators, verifications of the financial interests
     disclosure declarations, as well as checks for identifying actions damaging the prestige of the Judiciary and such related to
     impairment of the independence of judges, prosecutors and investigators; examine applications against an infringement of the
     right to have a case examined and disposed of within a reasonable time; draw up an annual programme for scheduled
     inspections and an annual report on the activity thereof, which it shall submit to the Plenum of the Supreme Judicial Council;
     adopt a template for reporting the completion of cases within the statutory time limits when carrying out its activity under Art. 54
     (1), item 2 of the JSA after consultations with the Supreme Judicial Council; summarize annually the good and bad practices
     regarding the observance of the ethical rules in accordance with the relevant European and international standards in
     connection with the abovementioned checks and shall provide the information to the Colleges of the Supreme Judicial Council.
     The ISJC carries out its inspections based on an annual program for the respective calendar year (planned inspections), upon
     signals and upon self-referral. The ISJC prepares an annual report on its activities, which is presented to the plenum of the
     Supreme Judicial Council and is considered by the National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria.

     Hungary
     Q070-1 (2022): The public prosecution services are led in a hierarchical structure. Leaders perform their duties at a national
     and regional level, as well as at the level of each organizational unit. It is up to the decision of the leader who exercises the
     employer’s rights to determine how the activities (performance, quality) of the prosecution office should be evaluated and on
     the basis of what indicators in order to manage the organizational unit effectively. The set of indicators may vary from year to
     year, depending on the circumstances. Therefore, more than one answer could be given to the given question.
     For example, the performance of individual prosecutors or officers may be assessed at the level of an organizational unit; a
     staff satisfaction survey may be conducted; or a target analysis based on client satisfaction may be carried out.
     The clearance rate could also be considered as a reference point and is actually monitored by the public prosecution services.
     However, statistics are produced at the level of the prosecution services and at the regional level on a calendar year basis.
     Therefore, those decisions on the termination of prosecution proceedings which are made at the end of a year, but become
     final only in the following year, can only be taken into account in the next year. The number of indictments and the number of
     finally closed cases that are closed because of finally closed court cases in the years after the indictment may also differ from
     the number of indictments on an annual basis. Therefore, the “clearance rate” – as a reference point – is a difficult criterion to
     follow.
     At the national level, the Prosecutor General is required to present a report to Parliament. This report does not focus on the
     performance of individual public prosecutors; instead, it assesses the performance of the public prosecution service as a whole
     and according to a breakdown of organizational units. In our 2023 response, we tried to take this into account and, in this
     respect, we have indicated that primarily the indicators indicated were taken into account. Compared to our previous response
     in 2020, there was no change in terms of the fact that the clearance rate had been taken into account, even if it was not the
     primary evaluation criterion.




     Q070-1 (2021): The BTM system (Criminal Justice Activity Indicator System) is available for the Prosecution Service of
     Hungary. This system reqularly monitors prosecution activities (performance and quality), however, it does not contain any
     information about the number of incoming cases, length of proceedings, number of resolved cases, backlogs etc.

     Ireland
     Q071 (2024): Civil Law statistics are recorded by cases received and cases resolved during the year. The majority of civil
     cases initiated in Ireland do not proceed to trial. Typically, they are settled between the parties (with or without a court
     approval), are formally discontinued (with notification to the defendant and the court), or are not pursued further by the plaintiff
     (without the plaintiff notifying the court). It is therefore not possible to provide figures for pending caseloads in most courts. In
     Criminal Law, backlogs can be measured when required.




     Q071 (2023): Civil Law statistics are recorded by cases received and cases resolved during the year. The majority of civil
     cases initiated in Ireland do not proceed to trial. Typically, they are either settled between the parties (with or without a court
     approving a settlement), are formally discontinued (involving notification to the defendant and the court), or are not pursued
     further by the plaintiff (without the plaintiff notifying the court). It is therefore not possible to provide figures for pending
     caseloads in most courts.
     In Criminal Law, cases are counted by offence, not by case/defendant. We record resolved cases as cases where an order is
     made. As there may be more than one penalty imposed in respect of an offence and a separate order made in respect of each
     penalty, the figures for resolved cases can appear to be higher than those for incoming cases and can cause difficulty in
     calculating figures for pending cases.

     Q072 (2024): The Inspectorate to the Supreme Judicial Council (ISJC):
     One of the main powers of the Inspectorate to the Supreme Judicial Council (ISJC) is to "check the organization of the
     initiation and progress of court, prosecution, and investigation cases, as well as the completion of cases within the established
     time limits" (Article 54, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Judiciary System Act). In exercising this power, the ISJC monitors for delays
     in the course of the relevant proceedings, which is done within the framework of the inspections carried out on the judicial
     authorities (comprehensive planned/scheduled inspections or inspections based on reports/signals) or when conducting
     preliminary investigations into reports/signals from individuals or legal entities of violations in the handling of cases. This year,
     the ISJC is responding to the questionnaire for the first time, as it has not been sent to it before. In previous years, the SJC
     probably gave a negative answer to this question in view of its own powers, rather than those exercised by the ISJC, which is
     an independent body separate from the SJC.

     Poland
     Q072 (General Comment): Public Prosecution services
     The issue of the duration of pre-trial proceedings is defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure, in Article 310 § 1 and § 2 and
     Article 325i § 1. Article 310 § 1 and § 2 states that the investigation shall be completed within 3 months. In justified cases the
     investigation period may be extended by a specified period of time by the public prosecutor supervising the investigation or the
     public prosecutor directly superior to the public prosecutor leading the investigation, but not longer than one year. In
     particularly justified cases a competent public prosecutor superior to the prosecutor supervising or leading the investigation
     may extend the investigation by a specified period of time.
     Article 325i § 1 states that an investigation should be completed within 2 months. The prosecutor may extend this period to 3
     months, and in particularly justified cases – to a longer specified period of time.
     The authority empowered to order the extension of an investigation or an inquiry by a specified period of time shall monitor
     such proceedings with respect to their proper conduct in view of their possible length and shall assess the validity of the
     procedural steps taken or to be taken.
     The request for the extension of an investigation or an inquiry must include the steps that need to be taken in the further
     course of the proceedings and indicate the reasons why they have not yet been taken.

CEPEJ study on the functioning of judicial systems

     Q083 (General Comment): Quantitative performance targets exist but they are not strictly binding. The Ministry of Justice in
     the Czech Republic uses "measures" (měřítka) as the sole numerical indicators for allocating judge and support staff positions
     across courts on an annual basis. Functioning similarly to case weights, these measures represent the notional number of
     cases that a judge or support staff member should handle in a year on a full-time basis; for example, in 2024, each district
     court judge is expected to manage 352 civil cases or 230 criminal cases annually. The measures are updated or confirmed
     each year by the systemisation commission, an informal body of representatives from regional, superior, and supreme court
     management, along with the Ministry of Justice. They are published in documents that accompany the Minister of Justice's
     annual allocation decision.
     Universal across courts of the same level, these measures and historical case data guide the Ministry in distributing judge and
     staff positions among superior, regional, and district courts. Regional court presidents have the flexibility to adjust these
     allocations based on local conditions or specific court needs, while staffing for the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative
     Court is managed through direct arrangements between their respective presidents and the Minister of Justice.
     To improve the accuracy of these allocations, the Ministry of Justice is undertaking a project, supported by the European
     Commission’s Technical Support Instrument, to gather empirical data on the labour intensity of various tasks performed by
     judges and support staff. This project aims to strengthen the factual basis for determining the measures.
     Additionally, court presidents continuously monitor the performance of judges and support staff to ensure cases are processed
     within reasonable timeframes, upholding individuals' right to have cases heard promptly. However, the Ministry of Justice does
     not regulate or oversee this managerial and disciplinary authority, which is independently exercised by court management.

     Q083-1-1 (2024): According to the Courts Act (Official Gazette No. 28/13, 33/15, 82/15, 67/18, 126/19, 130/20, 21/22, 60/22) ,
     the president of the court where a judge performs judicial duties issues a decision each calendar year assessing whether the
     judge has fulfilled their duties based on prescribed criteria. If it is determined that the judge, without justified reason, did not
     meet the required number of decisions or performed duties improperly, disciplinary proceedings must be initiated in
     accordance with the State Judicial Council Act.
     Disciplinary action against a court president is initiated by the president of the higher court. Sanctions for disciplinary offences
     may include a rebuke, salary reduction (up to one third for up to 12 months), or dismissal.
     If justified reasons exist for underperformance, they must be explained and the decision forwarded to the higher court. Judges
     may object to such a decision within three days; the court president must respond within eight days. If the objection is rejected,
     the judge may appeal to the higher court, whose decision is final and not subject to further legal remedies.




     Q083-1-1 (2023): According to the Courts Act (Official Gazette No. 28/13, 33/15, 82/15, 67/18, 126/19, 130/20, 21/22, 60/22)
     the president of the court in which the judge performs judicial duty determines by decision for the previous calendar year
     whether the judge has fulfilled his duties as a judge according to the prescribed criteria. If the president of the court determines
     that the judge, without justifiable reason, did not make the number of decisions determined by the Framework Criteria for the
     work of judges in a one-year period or that he performed his judicial duties improperly, he is obliged to initiate disciplinary
     proceedings against such a judge, in accordance with the State Judicial Council Act. Disciplinary proceedings against the
     president of the court are initiated by the president of the immediately higher court. According to the State Judicial Council Act
     (Official Gazette No. 116/10, 57/11, 130/11, 13/13, 28/13, 82/15, 67/18, 126/19, 80/22) disciplinary penalties may be imposed
     for committed disciplinary offences: rebuke, a fine of up to one third of the salary earned in the previous month in a period of
     one to three months, a fine of up to one third of the salary earned in the previous month in a period of four to six months, a fine
     of up to one third of the salary earned in the previous month in a period of seven to twelve months or dismissal from duty. If the
     president of the court determines that, due to justified reasons, the judge did not make the number of decisions determined by
     the Framework Criteria for the work of judges in a one-year period, he is obliged to state in the explanation of the decision what
     justified reasons are in question and submit the decision immediately to the president of the higher court. Against the decision
     of the president of the court, which determines whether the judge has fulfilled his duties as a judge, the judge can submit an
     objection to the president of the court within three days of receiving the decision. The president of the court is obliged to decide
     on the objection within eight days. The president of the court can reject the complaint or accept it and make a new decision. If
     the objection is rejected, the judge has the right to appeal to the president of the immediately higher court within eight days
     from the delivery of the decision on the objection. The president of the immediately higher court can make a decision
     confirming the decision of the president of the court or accept the appeal and make a new decision. Against this decision, the
     judge has no right to declare legal remedies.

     justified reasons are in question and submit the decision immediately to the president of the higher court.
     Against the decision of the president of the court, which determines whether the judge has fulfilled his duties as a judge, the
     judge can submit an objection to the president of the court within three days of receiving the decision.
     The president of the court is obliged to decide on the objection within eight days. The president of the court can reject the
     complaint or accept it and make a new decision.
     If the objection is rejected, the judge has the right to appeal to the president of the immediately higher court within eight days
     from the delivery of the decision on the objection. The president of the immediately higher court can make a decision
     confirming the decision of the president of the court or accept the appeal and make a new decision. Against this decision, the
     judge has no right to declare legal remedies.

     Poland
     Q083-3-1 (2024): *without disciplinary procedure:
     - Warning by head of prosecution
     In the event that the objectives of the criminal proceedings are not achieved or in the event that an obvious violation of the law
     is found in the conduct of the case, the superior public prosecutor shall, irrespective of his other powers, point out the
     misconduct to the public prosecutor who committed the misconduct, after requesting an explanation. The prosecutor to whom
     the misconduct has been pointed out may, within 7 days, submit a written objection to the superior prosecutor who pointed out
     the misconduct. If the public prosecutor does not agree with the infringement pointed out, he/she is entitled to appeal. If an
     objection is lodged, the superior public prosecutor who pointed out the misconduct shall either rescind the finding of
     misconduct or refer the case to the disciplinary court for consideration. The appeal procedure before the disciplinary court is
     then initiated.
     - Temporary salary reduction
     Without a disciplinary procedure, a salary reduction is not possible. A supervisor cannot decide on a pay cut alone.
     - Reflected in the individual assessment The whistleblowing notice shall be reflected in the prosecutor's personnel file. A copy
     of the notice of reproof that has not been rescinded shall be attached to the prosecutor's personnel file.
     - Other, please specify: _____
     For minor disciplinary offences that do not justify the initiation of disciplinary proceedings, the public prosecutor in charge shall
     inflict on subordinate public prosecutors an orderly penalty of admonition.
     A copy of the letter inflicted with an orderly penalty of admonishment shall be attached to the prosecutor's personal file. The
     public prosecutor to whom an admonishment by order penalty has been inflicted may, within 7 days from the date of service of
     the admonition, lodge an objection to the public prosecutor directly superior to the public prosecutor who inflicted the penalty.
     *With disciplinary procedure:
     -Warning by head of prosecution
     With the application of the disciplinary procedure, the initial route is the same as described above. Except that once the appeal
     procedure is triggered, the course of action is as follows. If an objection is lodged, the superior prosecutor who pointed out the
     misconduct shall either rescind the pointing out of the misconduct or refer the case to the disciplinary court for consideration.
     The disciplinary court shall issue an order upholding the reproof of misconduct or revoking the reproof of misconduct and
     discontinuing the proceedings after hearing the disciplinary ombudsman and the public prosecutor to whom the misconduct
     was reproved, unless a hearing is not possible. The prosecutor to whom the misconduct has been pointed out is entitled to
     lodge a complaint against the decision refusing to consider the objection. The complaint shall be examined by the same
     disciplinary court in another equivalent composition.
     - Temporary salary reduction
     A prosecutor may be suspended for up to 6 months if the nature of the disciplinary offence makes it necessary to immediately
     remove him or her from the performance of duties. In the case of a valid authorisation to prosecute a public prosecutor, and
     also when a request for incapacitation has been submitted to the competent court, the disciplinary supervisor may suspend the
     public prosecutor from his/her duties until the proceedings are validly concluded. The decision on suspension may be
     appealed to the Disciplinary Court of the Prosecutor General. Where a public prosecutor has been suspended, the Disciplinary




CEPEJ study on the functioning of judicial systems
in the EU Member States                                                                                                            171 / 1444
      Court at the Prosecutor General, on the motion of the disciplinary superior, may reduce the amount of the public prosecutor's
     salary up to 50% for the duration of the suspension. The decision on the reduction of remuneration may be appealed against.
     - Reflected in the individual assessment The whistleblowing notice shall be reflected in the prosecutor's personnel file. A copy
     of the notice of reproof that has not been rescinded shall be attached to the prosecutor's personnel file.
     - Other, please specify: _____
     A disciplinary penalty may be imposed on a prosecutor following a disciplinary procedure. The disciplinary penalties are: 1)
     admonishment; 2) reprimand; 2a) a 5% - 50% reduction in basic salary for a period of six months to two years; 2b) a pecuniary
     penalty in the amount of one month's basic salary payable for the month preceding the final conviction plus the prosecutor's
     long-term service allowance, function allowance and special allowance; 3) removal from the position held; 4) transfer to
     another official position;
     5) expulsion from the prosecution service. In the event of an appeal procedure against a warning, disciplinary proceedings
     shall be initiated. If an objection is lodged, the superior prosecutor: 1) repeals the disciplinary penalty of admonishment and
     notifies the prosecutor of the acceptance of the objection, or 2) overturns the disciplinary penalty of admonishment and refers
     the case to the disciplinary ombudsman for investigation, or 3) overturns the punishment of a caution and refers the case
     through the disciplinary ombudsman to the disciplinary court for examination. After the lapse of 3 years from the date on which
     the orderly penalty of admonishment becomes final, the Prosecutor General or the competent regional or district prosecutor
     shall order the removal of the copy of the letter of admonishment from the prosecutor's personal file, if during this period no
     misconduct in the efficiency of the pre-trial proceedings, the management of the prosecution or the exercise of supervision
     resulting in the drawing of attention, no misconduct was pointed out or no disciplinary offence was found to have been
     committed. In such a case, only the simultaneous. Removal from the prosecutor's personal file of copies of all such letters and
     judgments. At the request of the prosecutor, the removal may take place after one year. The decision of the disciplinary court
     may be appealed to the disciplinary court of the second instance.

     penalty in the amount of one month's basic salary payable for the month preceding the final conviction plus the prosecutor's
     long-term service allowance, function allowance and special allowance; 3) removal from the position held; 4) transfer to
     another official position;
     5) expulsion from the prosecution service. In the event of an appeal procedure against a warning, disciplinary proceedings
     shall be initiated. If an objection is lodged, the superior prosecutor: 1) repeals the disciplinary penalty of admonishment and
     notifies the prosecutor of the acceptance of the objection, or 2) overturns the disciplinary penalty of admonishment and refers
     the case to the disciplinary ombudsman for investigation, or 3) overturns the punishment of a caution and refers the case
     through the disciplinary ombudsman to the disciplinary court for examination. After the lapse of 3 years from the date on which
     the orderly penalty of admonishment becomes final, the Prosecutor General or the competent regional or district prosecutor
     shall order the removal of the copy of the letter of admonishment from the prosecutor's personal file, if during this period no
     misconduct in the efficiency of the pre-trial proceedings, the management of the prosecution or the exercise of supervision
     resulting in the drawing of attention, no misconduct was pointed out or no disciplinary offence was found to have been
     committed. In such a case, only the simultaneous. Removal from the prosecutor's personal file of copies of all such letters and
     judgments. At the request of the prosecutor, the removal may take place after one year. The decision of the disciplinary court
     may be appealed to the disciplinary court of the second instance.

     Austria
     Q120 (General Comment): In the Austrian judicial system we have diverse and multifaceted statistic products, which are an
     important basis for the management of justice. The statistics are regularly compiled by the Federal Computing Center and
     serve to control the deployment of personnel, but also for the supervision that is necessarily linked to the parties' right to a fair
     trial. The work of the public prosecutors is continuously and systematically reviewed on a quantitative level (i.e. number of
     completed cases, duration of proceedings). In this way, major deviations from the average can be identified. If a public
     prosecutor shows too many delays in proceedings or excessively long proceedings, this can lead to disciplinary proceedings or
     even a reduction in their job description. The assessment is carried out by the heads of the senior public prosecutors' offices. A
     qualitative assessment of each prosecutor’s work is carried out once for the second calendar year following their appointment
     to a specific position. The evaluation is repeated when they are appointed to a new position (for the second calendar year
     following that appointment). An assessment at a later time will be carried out, if either the head of the prosecutor’s office or the
     assessed prosecutor themselves have reason to believe that the result of the last assessment is no longer accurate. If the
     assessment finds the prosecutor’s work to be below average, the assessment is repeated for the next calendar year. The
     assessment is carried out by the personnel commission at the Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office, consisting of the Head of the
     Senior Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Head Prosecutor for the Public Prosecutor’s Office to which the assessed prosecutor
     belongs, one prosecutor appointed/chosen by the Union of Public Services and one prosecutor appointed/chosen by staff
     representatives.
     The evaluation takes into account the prosecutor’s professional abilities, skills, knowledge, conduct and performance. The
     assessment can be relevant for the prosecutor’s career, as it will be taken into account in later application procedures. If the
     assessment finds the prosecutor’s work failing to meet the absolute minimum peformance standards necessary to fulfill their
     duties for two consecutive calendar years, the prosecutor will be dismissed.

     The purpose of the assessment is to ensure quality control, but also to provide a form of coaching that contributes to the
     prosecutor’s development and to anticipate difficulties or a possible negative mention.
     Assessment also plays an essential role in consideration for a subsequent appointment or designation.
     Competent authorities:

     the general assembly or by the division assembly.

     of two heads of divisions from the public prosecutor's office, two magistrates who are members of the Opinion and
     Investigation Commission of the High Council of the Judiciary, a magistrate of the Court of Audit and a human resources

     Croatia
     Q120 (2024): State attorneys and deputy state attorneys are evaluated according to the following criteria:
     1. achieved results in resolving cases based on the number of cases assigned to work based on the Framework Criteria for the
     Work of Deputy State Attorneys and the average work results of county and municipal state attorneys' offices for the previous
     three-year period
     2. quality of decisions and justified use of legal remedies
     3. proper performance of state attorney duties - compliance with deadlines during the procedure
     4. other activities of the state attorney and deputy state attorney
     5. experience in performing state attorney duties
     6. compliance with the Code of Ethics for State Attorneys and Deputy State Attorneys.
     According to the above criteria, the state attorney and deputy state attorney can achieve a maximum of 150 points, whereby a
     maximum of 60 points can be achieved for the criteria stated in points 1 and 2, a maximum of 10 points for the criteria stated in
     points 3 and 4, and a maximum of five points for the criteria stated in points 5 and 6.
     The grades for the performance of the duties of the State Attorney and Deputy State Attorney are:
     1. excellent performance of the duties: 130 - 150 points
     2. very successful performance of the duties: 110 - 129 points
     3. successful performance of the duties: 90 - 109 points
     4. satisfactory performance of the duties: 70 - 89 points
     5. unsatisfactory performance of the duties: less than 70 points.
     The Deputy State Attorney is evaluated by the State Attorney, and the State Attorney is evaluated by the immediately superior
     State Attorney.
     The assessment must be reasoned. The state attorney and deputy state attorney who disagrees with the assessment have the
     right to file a complaint with the State Attorney Council.
     The assessment of the performance of the duties of a state attorney is taken into account in the procedures for the promotion
     and permanent transfer of deputy state attorneys and in the procedure for the appointment of state attorneys.
     To be appointed to the position of Deputy State Attorney in a higher state attorney's office, the Deputy State Attorney must be
     assessed at least with the grade "successfully performs his duties" in the last evaluation before appointment.

     Hungary
     Q120 (2024): In accordance with Section 50 (1) of Act CLXIV of 2011 on the Status and Career Path of the Prosecutor
     General, Prosecutors and other Prosecution Employees, prosecutors, with the exception of the prosecutor general and the
     deputy prosecutor general, shall be assessed before the expiry of the fixed term of the first prosecution appointment (for the
     purpose of appointment for an indefinite period), while in the case of a first appointment for an indefinite term, before the expiry
     of a period of three years following the appointment, and thereafter every eight years, provided that they worked under the
     supervision of the assessor or his/her deputy for a minimum of one year during the assessment period. The assessment is the
     responsibility of the person exercising the employer's authority.
     The purpose of assessment is to assess the quality of the prosecutor’s professional activities, to evaluate their skills, abilities
     and character traits with an impact thereon and to facilitate professional development. The assessment may only feature duly
     supported, factual findings.
     Prosecutors do not need to be assessed during the six years preceding the completion of the applicable old-age pension age.
     In addition to cases mentioned above, a prosecutor shall also be assessed if requested by the prosecutor, provided that two
     years have elapsed since the previous assessment, circumstances have emerged that indicate the prosecutor’s professional
     ineligibility or the necessity to alter the evaluation of the previous assessment.
     In the event of an ineligible grade, upon the disclosure of the result of the assessment, the prosecutor shall be called upon to
     resign his/her office within thirty days. If despite the call the prosecutor does not resign his/her office, his/her prosecution
     service employment shall be terminated by exempting him/her from office. If a prosecutor on fixed-term service is assessed as
     ineligible before the expiry of the fixed term, the prosecutor's service relationship shall be terminated on the date of expiry of
     the fixed term.
     In accordance with Sections 13/A-13/F of Instruction 4/2012. (I. 6.) of the Prosecutor General on specific questions regarding
     the status of employees of the Prosecution Service, a case file examination shall be carried out as a basis for the assessment
     which is due to follow with regard to prosecutors appointed to a prosecution office subordinated to the Office of the Prosecutor
     General prior to the time when the assessment is due. Such a case file examination shall not be carried out for senior head
     prosecutors. Case file examinations shall discover the examined prosecutor’s practice regarding the application of substantive
     and procedural law during at least a one-year period prior to the case file examination, or since the prosecutor’s latest
     assessment – or in absence of an assessment – since the time of his/her appointment. The case file examination and its
     evaluation shall be done by a prosecutor (hereinafter: examiner prosecutor) who works at the prosecution office directly
     superior to the prosecution office where the examined prosecutor is appointed to and who works in the same field of
     prosecutorial activity or expertise as the examined prosecutor. The examiner prosecutor shall be designated by the directly
     superior prosecution office, whereas at the Office of the Prosecutor General by the head of the structural unit that is competent
     regarding the examined prosecutor’s duties.
     In the future, the workload calculation system may also be suitable for quantitatively measuring and monitoring the work of




     prosecutors in the longer term, by performing calculations on an individual basis.

     the time for filing the documents (even in comparison with the other magistrates of the office); •work related publications, If

     prosecution, maintenance of state prosecution in court, as well as the protection of state and individual rights. An assessment

     suitability for the position. In the case of a negative opinion, the Commission can determine specific tasks that must be
     performed to eliminate the deficiencies found in prosecutor’s professional activity or to improve his/her professional activity.



     Q120 (2024): The purpose of evaluating professional performance of prosecutors is to promote the continuous professional
     development. The evaluation of the prosecutor's professional activity is carried out by the Attestation Commission of
     Prosecutors established by the Council of Prosecutor General at least once every five years. In cases where deficiencies are
     found in the prosecutor's professional activity, the assessment can be carried out any time before the term of five years. When
     evaluating the professional performance of the prosecutor, the Attestation Commission of Prosecutors analyses the quality of
     performance of the prosecutor's functions, the organization of individual work, the participation in activities improving
     qualification, the statistical indicators, as well as other criteria provided for in the Regulation on the Evaluation of Professional
     Performance of Prosecutors. Following the evaluation the Attestation Commission of Prosecutors gives a positive or negative
     opinion, in some cases specific tasks can be determined for the prosecutor to eliminate the deficiencies found in professional
     activity or to improve his professional performance. The opinion of the Attestation Commission of Prosecutors acquires legal
     force when it is approved by the Prosecutor General.



     Q120 (2023): The purpose of evaluating the professional performance of the prosecutor is to promote the continuous
     professional development of the prosecutor during the performance of his/her duties. The evaluation of the prosecutor's
     professional activity is carried out by the Attestation Commission of Prosecutors established by the Council of Prosecutor
     General at least once every five years. In cases where deficiencies are found in the prosecutor's professional activity, the
     assessment of his/her professional performance can be (in certain cases must be) carried out any time before the term of 5
     years. When evaluating the professional performance of the prosecutor, the Attestation Commission of Prosecutors analyses
     the quality of performance of the prosecutor's functions, the organization of individual work, participation in qualification raising
     events, statistical indicators of work, as well as other criteria provided for in the Regulation on the Evaluation of Professional
     Performance of Prosecutors. The Attestation Commission of Prosecutors gives a positive or negative opinion on the
     professional activity of the prosecutor, including, specific tasks can be determined for the prosecutor to be performed in order
     to eliminate the deficiencies found in his professional activity or to improve his professional performance. The opinion of the
     Attestation Commission of Prosecutors acquires legal force when it is approved by the Prosecutor General.

     Q120 (General Comment): On the proposal of the State Prosecutor General, State Prosecutorial Council adopts Criteria for

     Bulgaria
     Q120-1 (General Comment): Quantitative evaluation of the work of the prosecutors is carried out by applying the Rules for
     measuring the workload of the prosecutor's offices and the individual workload of each prosecutor and investigator, adopted by
     the Prosecution College/collegium of the SJC. It is possible to display the data according to the indicators provided for in the
     Rules in real time, both for the prosecutor's office as a whole, as well as for individual prosecutor's offices and for each specific
     prosecutor.
     Quantitative data on the workload are taken into account in the appraisal procedure of a specific prosecutor, in the course of
     which an assessment of his work is carried out, both in terms of quantitative indicators and also regarding the quality of the
     performed activity according to the results achieved.
     Prosecutors are assessed in accordance with Ordinance No. 3 of February 23, 2017 of the Supreme Judicial Council on the
     indicators and Methodology for Assessment and the Criteria for Reporting the Workload Degree of Prosecutors and
     Investigators and of Administrative Heads and Their Deputies (promulgated SG No. 21 /10.03.2017).
     Attestation is carried out:
     1. in advance - for a three-year period from the appointment to the position of prosecutor or investigator - when participating in
     a competition or when being offered a promotion;
     2. to acquire irreplaceability - upon completion of 5 years of experience as a prosecutor or investigator;
     3. periodically - for a 5-year period from the attestation of irreplaceability of a prosecutor and investigator, of an administrative
     head and of a deputy administrative head;
     4. extraordinary - in the cases under Art. 197, para. 5 of the Judicial System Act.
     Junior prosecutors and junior investigators are not assessed in advance, and a report on their work is prepared by the mentor
     in the second year of their appointment.

     Q120-1 (2021): Under Section 50 (1) of Act on Prosecutors, prosecutors shall be assessed on a regular basis, with the

     In case of the first appointment, which is for a definite term, the prosecutor shall be assessed by the end of that term. In case

     assessment, or in the occurrence of any circumstance which suggests professional inadequacy, or which necessitates the
     amendment of the results of the last assessment. The assessment procedure involves examination of case files, as set out in
     Sections 13A to 13F of the Prosecutor General's Order No. 4/2012.

     Q120-1 (2018): The evaluation system is defined by Articles 50-52 of the Act on the Legal Status of Prosecutors. The purpose
     is to assess the quality of the prosecutor’s activities, his/her skills, abilities and character traits with an impact thereon and to
     facilitate professional development. Prosecutors, with the exception of the Prosecutor General and the Deputy Prosecutor
     General, are assessed before the expiry of the fixed term of the first appointment, while in the case of a first appointment for an
     indefinite term, before the expiry of a period of 3 years following the appointment, and thereafter every 8 years. Prosecutors
     need not be assessed during the 6 years preceding the completion of the applicable old-age pension age. A prosecutor shall
     also be assessed if: requested by the prosecutor; circumstances have emerged that indicate the prosecutor’s professional
     ineligibility or the necessity to alter the evaluation of the previous assessment; in the extraordinary proceeding to be completed
     without delay, s/he fails to meet the deadline extended by the superior prosecutor. The assessment is the duty of the person
     exercising the employer’s rights. The official work of prosecutors assigned to the Ministry is evaluated by the Minister
     responsible for justice in accordance with the rules applicable to government officials. As a result, prosecutors may be
     awarded the following grades: excellent, suitable for promotion; excellent and fully eligible; eligible; eligible, subsequent
     assessment required; ineligible. In the event of an ineligible grade, the prosecutor shall be called upon to resign his/her office
     within thirty days. If the prosecutor is awarded a grade “eligible, subsequent assessment required”, the person exercising the
     employer’s rights identifies the deficiencies and irregularities and states the main criteria of the desired changes which shall be
     reviewed prior to the next assessment (within 2 years). A prosecutor shall be awarded an ineligible grade upon the next
     assessment if he/she fails to obtain an eligible grade. S/he may request a court of law to quash any erroneous or untrue
     finding.

     Q120-1 (2024): In general, no less than once every five years, if all skills are assessed at an appropriate level. If deficiencies
     are found in the actions of the prosecutor and the measures taken have not brought positive results, then the assessment is
     carried out earlier. If the prosecutor's skills are assessed negatively, the evaluation must be carried out immediately. As from
     2024, a new system of the evaluation of prosecutors is introduced, which also provides for annual evaluation. In accordance
     with this new system, starting from the reporting period of 2023, an annual evaluation of the activities of district-level
     prosecutors is carried out – the results of the activities of all district-level prosecutors in four main work areas are compared
     with each other:
     – supervision of criminal cases under investigation,
     – completion of the pre-trial investigation,
     – maintenance of state prosecution in court,
     – work in the field of non-criminal cases.
     Each of the mentioned areas is evaluated according to the performance indicators, which are grouped into three categories –
     quantity, quality and compliance with the strategic goals of the Prosecution Office. As a result of the evaluation, prosecutors
     are divided into three groups – good efficiency, satisfactory efficiency (minor improvements necessary), unsatisfactory
     efficiency (significant improvements necessary). Regarding prosecutors that are evaluated as working satisfactorily, their direct
     managers set development goals for them for the current year. Regarding prosecutors that are evaluated as working
     unsatisfactory, the responsible structural unit of the Prosecutor General’s Office creates a professional development program
     with performance improvement tasks for the current year. The execution of this program is controlled by the prosecutor's
     immediate supervisor and/or a higher-ranking prosecutor. For the period from 2023, in relation to chief prosecutors
     (organizational management) and higher-ranking prosecutors, a 360-degree performance and competence evaluation is
     carried out using survey questionnaires. The results of the survey are sent to the corresponding next level chief prosecutors
     and next higher-ranking prosecutors. Based on the survey results, they set professional development goals for their chief
     prosecutors and lower-ranking prosecutors for the current year.

     Austria
     Q042 (2024): In 2024 in Austria, the number of courts considered as legal entities is 150. Namely, there are 131 courts of
     general jurisdiction and 19 specialised courts. Among the 131 legal entities of general jurisdiction, 126 act at first instance, 4 at
     second instance and one at third instance. More precisely, the 113 District courts and the 13 Regional courts of general
     jurisdiction intervene as first instance courts. It is noteworthy that the 6 other regional and 1 district court that have specialised
     jurisdiction are not taken into consideration here, but are counted as specialised first instance courts (infra). It is to be
     mentioned that the peculiarity of the 20 Austrian Regional courts is that even though these are first instance courts, some of
     them are also competent in respect of appeals against District courts’ decisions. The 4 Higher Regional Courts have appeal
     competence in respect of all civil and criminal cases. The Supreme court is the highest instance court in civil and criminal
     matters.

     Belgium
     Q042 (General Comment): The reform of the Justices of the peace, involving a reduction in geographic locations, was
     consolidated by the law of 25th December 2017. The implementation of the reform took place between 2016 and 2019.

     “1.1 First instance courts of general jurisdiction - legal entities”: 13 first-instance courts, 162 Justices of the peace and 15
     police courts. As for the assize courts governed by Articles 114 et seq. of the Judicial Code, due to their specific nature, they
     are not considered legal entities within the meaning of the CEPEJ and are not included in the table. In principle, the assize
     court sits in the capital of the various provinces and in the administrative district of Brussels-Capital. Thus, it sits in Antwerp,
     Arlon, Bruges, Brussels, Ghent, Liège, Leuven, Mons, Namur, Nivelles, or Tongeren, depending on the circumstances (Article
     115 of the Judicial Code). There are therefore 11 assize courts in Belgium.

     “1.2 Second instance courts of general jurisdiction - legal entities” : there are five appellate courts ; however, it should be
     mentioned that the 13 first-instance courts also act as appellate courts with regard to decisions made by the justices of the
     peace.

     Starting from 2022, both justices of the peace and police courts are included under courts of general jurisdiction. In previous
     cycles, they were categorized as specialized first-instance courts. The assize courts were taken into account from 2020 to
     2023, but starting from 2024, due to their specific nature (they do not sit permanently) they are no longer included in the table
     as first instance courts of general jurisdiction.

     Given that the Council of State (Conseil d'Etat) acts both at first instance level and on appeal, it has been accounted for under
     both columns Q43 but only once within the total of Q42.2.



     Q042 (2024): Point “1.2 Second instance courts of general jurisdiction - legal entities”: only the five courts of appeal are listed

     instance.” From 2024 onwards, due to their specific nature, the 11 assize courts that do not sit permanently are no longer

     Q042 (2020): Judiciary System Act
     Article 65
     All courts are legal entities funded by the budget and shall be represented by the administrative head or another designated
     person. In the discharge of the functions of administrative head, orders, instructions and rules shall be issued in accordance
     with the statutory competence. The general assembly, the plenum of the Supreme Cassation Court and the Plenum of the
     Supreme Administrative Court shall be bodies of the respective court, which rule only in the cases specified in the law, give
     opinions, adopt rules and decisions by open ballot and a majority of more than half of the judges present.

     courts as well as the number of municipal state attorneys’ offices has been reduced continued in 2019 with the merger of
     municipal and misdemeanour courts into municipal courts.
     The reasons for the merger were a significant decrease in the number of misdemeanour cases and overburdened municipal
     courts with civil cases. In the new judicial map, instead of 46 municipal and misdemeanour courts, there are now 34 municipal
     courts - all misdemeanour and municipal courts were merged in the same cities except in 2 largest cities, Zagreb and Split, in
     which specialised municipal courts for misdemeanour cases were retained, and due to geographical specificities and size of
     certain municipal courts they were separated and new municipal courts were established (10). Also, a new commercial court
     was established in Dubrovnik. The aim of this new judicial map with new courts in the network and increased jurisdiction of
     permanent services is to increase the efficiency of the courts, improve access to court services, ensure even distribution of the
     workload of judges, shorten the length of court proceedings, reduce the number of unresolved cases in municipal courts, and
     ensure optimisation and easier management of human resources in courts.

     Q043 (General Comment): With regard to the Enforcement of criminal sanctions courts: in matters of enforcement of
     sentences, the enforcement judge (JAP) is a court of first instance for the enforcement of sentences, being at the same time a
     decision-making, control and monitoring body. There is at least one JAP per department (article 712-2 of the CPP). The JAP is
     competent for adult convicts, and his/her field of intervention is the following: for measures to individualize custodial sentences,
     he or she has general jurisdiction (except for a few measures that fall under the special jurisdiction of the Court for the
     enforcement of sentences); for custodial sentences, when a specific text so provides; for the follow-up of security measures.
     Established by the law of March 9, 2004, the Court for the enforcement of sentences (TAP) is a court of first instance,
     composed of three JAPs of first instance courts, appointed by order of the First President of the Appelate Court. In each
     Appelate Court, a TAP is established whose territorial jurisdiction extends to the jurisdiction of this court (articles 712-3 and D
     49-2 of the CPP, article indicating the list of TAPs by Appelate court and the territorial jurisdiction). The seat of the TAP is in
     principle "that of the first instance court of the seat of the Appelate Court" (article D. 49-3 CPP).
     The objective is to entrust the most complex and sensitive cases to a collegiality. Thus, the TAP has jurisdiction over: 1) by the
     effect of the law for those sentenced to the heaviest penalties: applications for parole and suspension of "medical" sentences
     for persons sentenced to imprisonment of more than 10 years and whose remaining sentence to be served exceeds 3 years;
     applications for an increase in the security period; placement under judicial supervision of dangerous persons...); 2) by
     decision of the JAP, in particular due to the complexity of the case or the personality of the convicted person (article 712-6 al 3
     of the CPP), this referral to the collegiality may be made ex officio or at the request of the convicted person or the public
     prosecutor.
     In terrorism matters, there is a derogation from ordinary law (articles 706-22-1 and D 49-75 to D49-81-5 of the Criminal
     Procedure Code). The Paris sentence enforcement courts specialising in terrorist matters (JAPAT, TAPAT and the sentence
     enforcement chamber) have: exclusive jurisdiction to monitor persons convicted by specialised terrorism courts pursuant to
     article 706-17 of the Criminal Procedure Code; concurrent jurisdiction with ordinary courts for the enforcement of sentences to
     monitor persons convicted of acts of terrorism and other offences falling within the scope of article 706-16 of the Criminal
     Procedure Code by ordinary courts.
     source DACG.

     Germany
     Q042 (General Comment): Even though the German legal system generally knows three instances (first instance, appeal on
     questions of fact and law, appeal on questions of law only), the different kinds of courts do not correspond directly to the
     stages of appeal. Local courts (Amtsgerichte) are first instance courts with the regional courts (Landgerichte) as next stage of
     appeal (exceptions apply in family matters). However, regional courts do not only serve as second instance courts but also
     deal with first instance cases. Whether a case is initially dealt with at a local or regional court depends (among other things) on
     the value at dispute (civil cases) or on the kind of the suspected offence (criminal cases). Similarly the higher regional courts
     may serve as second instance courts (for cases that were initially dealt with at regional courts or for cases in family matters)
     and as highest instance courts for cases that were initiated at the local courts (especially in criminal cases). In some specific
     cases, higher regional courts may also be courts of first instance.
     The constitutional courts of the federal states and the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) are not part of
     the stages of appeal. Constitutional jurisdiction is also seen as separate from general and specialised jurisdiction.
     Constitutional courts review legislation with regard to constitutional provisions. The Federal Constitutional Court mainly assess
     alleged violations of base rights by public authorities. However, in order to have access to the constitutional courts, the regular
     path of legal proceedings must generally be exhausted.

     Q043 (General Comment): It is noteworthy that depending on the value at dispute, commercial cases are dealt with at local or
     regional courts, on application in a chamber established at the regional court for commercial cases. There are no separate
     commercial courts. Likewise, there are no independent rent and tenancies courts, enforcement courts or courts for insurance
     cases. Depending on the caseload, special panels of judges are established for this purpose at the local and regional Courts.
     Family cases are dealt with at first instance in special departments of the local courts (second instance: higher regional
     courts). The Federal Armed Forces do not have any military courts of their own; its members are generally subject to civil
     jurisdiction.The federal military disciplinary courts are first instance courts of administrative jurisdiction for disciplinary
     proceedings against members of the armed forces. The second and highest instance court for isciplinary proceedings against
     members of the armed forces is the Federal Administrative Court.
     Juvenile courts do not exist as independent courts either. They are established at the local courts or regional courts,
     depending on the severity of the expected sentence and the type of offence. The juvenile courts may be composed of a single
     criminal judge sitting as youth judge or one or more judges together with lay youth assessors.

     Greece
     Q042 (2024): Τhe consolidation of magistrates’ and first instance courts resulted in the abolition of all magistrates’courts.Τhe
     magistrates’ court courthouses, which were located in the same places as the first instance courts have been closed down.
     Their facilities are now serving as additional installations for the relevant first instance courts.As regards the 50 magistrates’
     courts, these have been transformed into regional seats for the first instance courts, while the remaining have been closed.
     The basic principle of the new spatial restructuring of the courts is that each regional unit (former administrative “Prefecture”)
     will have a central Court of First Instance, to which all the judges of this Prefecture (former Magistrates’’ as well as First
     Instance Court Judges) will receive permanent positions. Exceptions are valid for border regions or island regions due to
     constitutional provisions (thus prefectures in Thrace, Northern Macedonia, Western Macedonia regions and Aegean islands,
     where the rule of one first instance court per administrative prefecture does not apply) .
     The total number of the First Instance Courts in Greece before the adoption of Law 5108/2024 was 63. 56 of them are now
     First Instance Courts and 7 that are considered as “parallel” court seats to the (central) Courts - since there were previously
     some Prefectures where two or more First Instance Courts co-existed, providing full jurisdiction. Thus, delocalization and
     simplification of the first instance is achieved and, at the same time, better and more direct access to justice for citizens is
     provided. According to the new framework, lawyers and citizens can submit documents/claims either to the central or the
     regional/parallel courts (not independent judicial structures), since there is only one first Instance court in each administrative
     Prefecture, served by one or more premises.

     Q043 (General Comment): In Greece, there are no special courts for the fields of law described in the question 43, besides
     those already mentioned. The Greek Constitution is reluctant to provide in the Greek legal system special courts. Instead,
     within the Courts of First Instance and Courts of Appeal of large cities, we have special Chambers, where the task of
     adjudicating in special categories of law (e.g. family law, commercial law, etc.) is assigned. Judges entrusted with such duties
     have usually the correspondent specific studies. As far as other special courts are concerned, special provisions regulate the

     Ireland has a specialist regime for the trial of commercial proceedings in the form of the Commercial List of the High Court
     (known as the 'Commercial Court') but, as it is not a separate legal entity, being a list within and formally a part of the High
     Court, it is not included as a specialist court as such.
     The Labour Court in Ireland is a tribunal rather than a court of law, which is why it is not included in the table of Q43. It cannot
     award costs; instead, it hears both sides of a case and issues non-binding recommendations. While these recommendations
     are expected to be given serious consideration, the responsibility for resolving disputes ultimately rests with the parties
     involved.

     Family High Court, Family Circuit Court and Family District Court as divisions of the existing court jurisdictions and provides for

     Q043 (General Comment): Since 2014 in Italy there are 22 Brand Commercial courts (Tribunali delle imprese) that are legal
     entities of their own and not just internal court divisions for organizational purpose (such as labour, family etc.).
     Notably, in Italy, some specialised first-instance courts are not administered or financed by the Ministry of Justice. These
     include regional audit commissions, local tax commissions and military courts. As a result, these courts are not considered in
     responses regarding court budgets, cases, judges, or non-judge staff. Regional audit commissions are not even counted in the
     number of courts. Conversely, regional administrative courts (first-instance administrative courts) and the supreme
     administrative court, although they are also not administered or financed by the Ministry of Justice, are included in the counts.
     Since 2014, they have been considered in the totals for the number of courts and cases. Additionally, starting from 2018, they
     have been included in the counts for the number of judges, non-judge staff and in the courts budget.
     Moreover, in Italy specific matters (such as labour, family etc.) are dealt by specific divisions within the same Court. There are
     also 26 divisions called DDA (Direzioni Distrettuali Antimafia) which deal specifically with mafia and organized crime.

     Luxembourg
     Q042 (General Comment): 42.1.1: three justices of the peace and two district courts

     42.1.2: one Court of Appeal 42.1.3: one Court of Cassation

     42.2: Total specialized courts (all instances) In addition to the actual jurisdictions, the law of July 27, 1997 organizing the
     Constitutional Court established this court which is seized, as a preliminary ruling, when a question arises regarding the
     conformity of a law with the Constitution before a judicial or administrative jurisdiction.

     It rules by way of judgment on laws' conformity with the Constitution, except for those approving treaties.

     When one party raises an issue concerning a law's compliance with the Constitution before either judicial or administrative
     jurisdiction, that jurisdiction must refer it to The Constitutional Court unless it considers that making a decision on the raised
     issue is unnecessary for its judgment; that such question lacks any foundation; or that The Constitutional Court has already
     ruled on an identical matter.

     If any jurisdiction deems there’s an issue about whether certain legislation complies with constitutional provisions and deciding
     upon this point is necessary for delivering its verdict then it should raise this matter ex officio after previously inviting parties to
     present their observations.

     Parties are entitled to conclude and plead before the Constitutional Court through representation by a counsel listed in
     Category I annually compiled tables set up by bar councils’ orders."

     The judgments of the Constitutional Court are published in the Official Journal of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg within thirty
     days from their pronouncement." (Justice Portal : https://justice.public.lu/fr/organisation-justice/cour-constitutionnelle.html)

     Q042 (2022): In addition to the regular courts, the Law of 27 July 1997 on the organization of the Constitutional Court,
     established this court, which is seized for a preliminary ruling when a question arises before a judicial or administrative
     jurisdiction concerning the conformity of a law with the Constitution. It rules by way of judgment on the conformity of laws with
     the Constitution, except those approving treaties.



     When a party raises an issue regarding compliance of a law with the Constitution before a judicial or administrative jurisdiction,
     that jurisdiction is required to refer it to the Constitutional Court, unless it considers that deciding on such matter is not
     necessary for its judgment, that there are no grounds for such issue or that there has already been an decision by the
     Constitutional Court on an identical matter.



     If any jurisdiction deems that an issue relating to compliance of a law with the Constitution arises and a decision on this point is
     necessary for its judgment, it must raise it ex officio after having previously invited the parties to present their observations.



     The parties are entitled to conclude and plead before the Constitutional Court through a counsel registered in List I annually
     drawn up by the councils of bar associations.

     Judgments from the Constitutional Court are published in the Official Gazette of Luxembourg within thirty days from their
     pronouncement. (Justice Portal: https://justice.public.lu/fr/organisation-justice/cour-constitutionnelle.html)




     Q042 (2020): "In addition to the courts proper, the law of 27 July 1997 on the organization of the Constitutional Court
     established this court, which is seized, on a preliminary basis, when a question relating to the conformity of a law to the
     Constitution arises before a court of the judicial or administrative order. It rules, by means of a judgment, on the conformity of
     laws with the Constitution, with the exception of those concerning the approval of treaties.
     When a party raises a question concerning the conformity of a law with the Constitution before a court of the judicial or
     administrative order, that court is obliged to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court, except when it considers that a
     decision on the question raised is not necessary to render its judgment, that the question is unfounded or that the
     Constitutional Court has already ruled on a question with the same object.
     If a court considers that a question of conformity of a law with the Constitution arises and that a decision on this point is
     necessary to render its judgment, it must raise it of its own motion after first inviting the parties to present their observations.
     The parties are admitted to conclude and plead before the Constitutional Court through the ministry of a lawyer registered in
     list I of the tables drawn up annually by the Bar Associations.
     The judgments of the Constitutional Court are published in the Official Journal of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg within thirty
     days of their delivery. (Portal of Justice: https://justice.public.lu/fr/organisation-justice/cour-constitutionnelle.html) "

     Q042 (General Comment): Second instance courts of general jurisdiction handle civil, criminal and tax cases.
     There are two additional courts that do not seem to fit this categorization by instance, acting in the area of administrative law.
     Some administrative law cases (tax cases) are handled by first and second instance courts of general jurisdiction. Other
     administrative cases are handled by the Trade and Industry Appeals Tribunal, also known as the Administrative High Court for
     Trade and Industry (College van van Beroep voor het Bedrijfsleven). This is a specialized administrative court, which rules on
     disputes in the area of social-economic administrative law, and appeals for specific laws. The tribunal hears both first and
     second instance cases. Categorized as a specialized court.
     The Central Appeals Tribunal (Centrale Raad van Beroep) is a court of appeal mainly active in legal areas pertaining to social
     security and civil service. In these areas, it is also the highest judicial authority. In some cases, it is the first and sole instance.
     This court does not exactly fit the distinction of the table above, but categorized as a specialized court.
     The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State is the highest administrative court with general jurisdiction in the
     Netherlands. It hears various types of appeals (e.g. members of the public / associations / commercial companies against
     governmental bodies, or between public authorities). This court does not exactly fit the distinction of the table above, but
     categorized as a specialized court. For more information, see https://www.rechtspraak.nl/English/Judicial-system-and-
     legislation/Pages/Special-Tribunals.aspx. Note that the Supreme Court (highest instance court of general jurisdiction) does not
     retry the case itself, but judges whether the judges at the first and second instance applied the law correctly in the judgment,
     and whether the procedure was correctly followed (cassation, potential quashing of judgment).
     Since 2013 and following the implementation of the reform related to the reorganization of the judicial map, the number of
     district courts was reduced from 19 in 2010 to 11 in 2013 and 2014. Moreover, this reform resulted in the closure of sub-district
     court locations due to which the number of geographic locations decreased from 64 in 2010 to 40 in 2013 and 2014.

     Poland
     Q042 (General Comment): The Polish court structure is characterized by four levels of courts but only three instances.
     Basically, there are district courts which are first instance courts, regional courts which are first and second instance courts
     (regional courts within their jurisdiction have the majority of first-instance cases), and appellate courts which are second
     instance courts. The highest instance courts are the Supreme Court, the Supreme Administrative Court and the Constitutional
     Tribunal.

     functioned from 2004 until the creation of intellectual property courts, which took place on 1 July 2020. Cases in the field of
     intellectual property belong to the jurisdiction of selected District Courts (Article 47990 of the Code of Civil Procedure), while
     the District Court in Warsaw (XXII Division) has exclusive jurisdiction in matters of intellectual property concerning computer
     programs, inventions, utility models, topography of integrated circuits, plant varieties and company secrets of a technical
     nature.
     The Court of Competition and Consumer Protection is a special department functioning within the District Court in Warsaw. In
     the current state of law, the scope of activity of the 17th Department of the Court of Competition and Consumer Protection
     includes the handling of the following cases in court proceedings of appeals and complaints against decisions and orders
     issued by the government: the President of the Office of Competition and Consumer Protection, the President of the Energy
     Regulatory Office, the President of the Railway Transport Office, the President of the Office of Electronic Communications.
     When it comes to matters from lease or tenancy agreements - as long as these matters are of an economic nature, they are
     recognized by business departments, as are matters related to new technologies and the Internet space.

     Q043 (General Comment): In the Slovak court system there are 8 Regional courts which are the courts with dual competence.
     The Regional courts are the courts of appeal with the general jurisdiction in the civil, commercial and the criminal cases. In the
     appellate procedure they decide the appeals lodged against the decisions of all 54 District courts within their local jurisdiction.
     At the same time the Regional courts have the jurisdiction as the courts of first instance in administrative matters. They act as
     the administrative courts.
     The Specialized Criminal court is competent to judge the grave criminal matters enumerated in the § 14 of the Criminal
     procedure Code (e. g. premeditated murder, corruption, terrorism, organised crime, severe economic crimes, damaging the
     financial interests of the EU etc.). Highest instance courts are the Supreme Court, Supreme Administrative Court and the
     Constitutional Court.

     courts. These 8 general regional courts are already legal entities included in Q42, line 1.2. Highest instance courts are the
     Supreme Court and the new Supreme Adminstrative Court.

     (CEPEJ(2013)7) the change should be gradual. The reduction in the number of courts regarding geographical locations is not
     foreseen, but reorganization in the powers of local courts that are organizational units of district courts might be needed. There
     are local courts that have only a few (3-5) judges, which is not rational in the sense of court management. Such local courts
     might start dealing only with certain kinds of cases, with other local courts in the same district dealing with other kinds of
     cases, having de facto specialized local courts.
     Nevertheless, these changes are still in the initial debate phase, so no formal proposal can be presented yet.

     Q044 (2018): The traditional structure of a Court includes a Judge (or Magistrate), a Judicial Counsellor, and several civil
     servants (the exact number depends on many circumstances). The New Judicial Office (Nueva Oficina Judicial)has been
     implemented in many territories and its development continues. The New Judicial Office (NOJ) has, as base, the called
     ‘Procedural Unit of Direct Support' (UPAD), a small office with personnel necessary for the strict aid of the work of the Judge.
     On the other hand, and for the uniform processing of repetitive tasks, the called Common Procedural Services have been
     created. The Judicial Counsellor is the Director of these services, and is responsible of processing the phase of the judicial file
     of a strictly procedural nature.

     Q044 (2016): The traditional structure of a Court includes a Judge (or Magistrate), a Lawyer of the Administration of Justice,
     and several civil servants (the exact number depends on many circumstances). The New Judicial Office (Nueva Oficina
     Judicial) has been implemented in many territories and its development continues. The New Judicial Office (NOJ) has, as
     base, the called ‘Procedural Unit of Direct Support' (UPAD), a small office with personnel necessary for the strict aid of the
     work of the Judge. On the other hand, and for the uniform processing of repetitive tasks, the called Common Procedural
     Services have been created. The Lawyer of the Administration of Justice is the Director of these services, and is responsible of
     processing the phase of the judicial file of a strictly procedural nature.

     new model of collegial courts aimed at replacing local courts belonging to the same judicial district.

     competence in respect of all civil and criminal cases. The Supreme court is the highest instance court in civil and criminal

     Germany
     Q042 (General Comment): Even though the German legal system generally knows three instances (first instance, appeal on
     questions of fact and law, appeal on questions of law only), the different kinds of courts do not correspond directly to the
     stages of appeal. Local courts (Amtsgerichte) are first instance courts with the regional courts (Landgerichte) as next stage of
     appeal (exceptions apply in family matters). However, regional courts do not only serve as second instance courts but also
     deal with first instance cases. Whether a case is initially dealt with at a local or regional court depends (among other things) on
     the value at dispute (civil cases) or on the kind of the suspected offence (criminal cases). Similarly the higher regional courts
     may serve as second instance courts (for cases that were initially dealt with at regional courts or for cases in family matters)
     and as highest instance courts for cases that were initiated at the local courts (especially in criminal cases). In some specific
     cases, higher regional courts may also be courts of first instance.
     The constitutional courts of the federal states and the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) are not part of
     the stages of appeal. Constitutional jurisdiction is also seen as separate from general and specialised jurisdiction.
     Constitutional courts review legislation with regard to constitutional provisions. The Federal Constitutional Court mainly assess
     alleged violations of base rights by public authorities. However, in order to have access to the constitutional courts, the regular
     path of legal proceedings must generally be exhausted.
