     Criminal Proceedings of the Unified Investigation Authority and Prosecution Service Criminal Statistics System (hereinafter
     ENyÜBS-BBS). In the ENyÜBS-BBS subsystem, the data is recorded when the investigating authorities or the Prosecution
     Service have made a procedural decision giving reasons for the provision of statistical data in connection with the crime (e.g.:
     dismissal of the criminal complaint, termination, suspension, accusation/indictment), relating to which statistical data was
     provided. Considering the time of data recording, the ENyÜBS-BBS subsystem is, therefore, of a so-called follow-up nature, so
     it does not show how many crimes occurred in the year under review, but it shows how many legal decisions were made in
     connection with such acts and in how many cases statistical data was provided in this context (in a registrative manner). As a
     result, the above also means that it may occur there is an ongoing criminal proceeding that is not included in the ENyÜBS
     database yet. For the questions "Pending cases on 1 Jan. ref. year" and "Pending cases on 31 December ref.year" in the
     table, please note that no data is collected on the number of pending cases – on a given day – into the records of the

     Q107-1 (2024): Discrepancy explanation:
     Based solely on data analysis, it can be stated that the number of defendants affected by final court decisions decreased by
     3.8% in 2024 compared to the previous year (2,156 defendants). Thus, as can be seen from the other data sets, there has
     been a general decrease in the number of defendants.
     If we examine the ratios of the two legal institutions (acceptance of confessions made at preparatory hearings; acceptance of
     confessions made at first instance trials), a kind of restructuring can be observed.
     In 2023, compared to all defendants affected by final judgments, the acceptance of confessions made at the preparatory
     hearing by the court accounted for 21.4%, while the acceptance of confessions made at the first instance trials by the court
     accounted for 2.2% of the cases. The same figures for 2024 were 21.9% and 1.7%, respectively. It can therefore be concluded
     from the above that although the number of defendants decreased in both data sets, proportionally more defendants made
     confessions and had them accepted by the court during the preparatory proceedings than during the first instance trial.
     Thus, it can be concluded that, looking solely at the ratios, proportionally more defendants made confessions during the
     preparatory proceedings, which were accepted by the court, and this presumably led to a decrease in the number of
     defendants who made confessions during the first-instance trial.
     In general, the prosecution service has no influence on how many defendants make confessions during court proceedings in a
     given year, or at what stage of the proceedings they do so.

     Q107 (2024): Increase in Cases Brought to Court (Section 3.3):
     In 2024, prosecutors took over 4,057 criminal proceedings involving particularly significant offenses. Compared to 2022, this
     represents a 40.3% increase. This rise is partly due to the reclassification of certain crimes as high-priority, such as violations
     of international and national sanctions, illegal border crossings, human smuggling, and facilitating unlawful residence in Latvia.
     Additionally, the number of cases submitted for prosecution involving these offenses increased significantly—from 454 in 2023
     to 975 in 2024—reflecting both improved investigative efforts and enhanced prosecutorial oversight.
     Decrease in Cases Concluded by Prosecutorial Penalty or Measure (Section 3.2):
     Contrary to previous years, where a growing number of cases were concluded within the prosecution, 2024 saw a notable
     decline. This shift is primarily due to amendments to the Criminal Law (effective July 4, 2024), which changed sentencing
     policies for certain categories of offenses—especially those involving violence or committed under the influence of alcohol or
     drugs in traffic incidents. These amendments removed alternative penalties such as community service and fines, leaving only
     probation supervision as an option. As a result, for offenses committed between July 4 and December 31, 2024, prosecutors
     could not conclude proceedings without referring the cases to court. This led to a significant increase in cases brought to court
     and a decrease in those resolved by prosecutorial penalty.

     Luxembourg
     Q107 (2024): 3.1.1 Between 2023 and 2024, a significant 26% increase was observed in resolved cases by the public
     prosecutor because the offender could not be identified. This development is part of a broader trend, marked by a continuous
     rise in the number of incoming cases registered by the public prosecutor’s offices in recent years. Since 2022, the proportion of
     cases with an unknown perpetrator has regularly exceeded 40% of the total cases handled.

     This situation is partly explained by the growing prevalence of cybercrime, which represents an increasing share of
     discontinued cases without further action. Prosecution in this area is particularly complex due to the technical nature of the
     offenses and their often international scope, making it difficult or even impossible to identify the perpetrators.

     Moreover, this increase also affects other categories of offenses, such as scams, frauds, and the intentional destruction or
     damage of movable property. In these cases as well, the absence of elements allowing for the identification of perpetrators
     prevents any judicial proceedings, thereby contributing to the rise in discontinued cases without further action.

     imposed by the warning or fulfils its obligations arising from the mediation.
     In the event of non-compliance, the public prosecution will resume.
     3.1.4: These mainly concern two specific measures: firstly, with regard to road traffic, the obligation to follow a driving course
     and, only for young adult offenders, participation in a course in the Choice 18+ programme designed to prevent drug addiction
     (https://www.solina.lu/fr/facilities/impuls/).
     The drop in cases closed for Other reasons is explained by the drop in cases closed involving young adult offenders (aged 18
     to 21). If these young offenders take part in a course as part of the Choice 18+ programme, designed to prevent drug
     addiction, and successfully complete it, their cases are closed. However, for reasons of internal organisation within the public
     prosecutor's offices, these cases are not closed as and when a traineeship is completed, but as a group, i.e. when a certain
     threshold of completed traineeships is reached. Finally, the drop in closed cases recorded since 2023 in the area of narcotics
     and concerning young offenders can be explained by the legalisation of recreational cannabis in Luxembourg in July 2023 and
     the subsequent drop in prosecutions by law enforcement.

     possible, given preference to the procedure of judgement by agreement (procédure du jugement sur accord), as it requires
     less physical presence of parties, defence counsel, witnesses, etc. Moreover, since the procedure of judgment by agreement
     was only introduced in 2015, the habit of resorting to this measure has only become established in recent years among
     lawyers, who now take the initiative themselves more often to launch this procedure.

     the guilty plea procedure, since it does not require the same amount of physical presence of the parties, the defenders,
     witnesses, etc.

     Q107 (General Comment): The number of pending cases at the end of the year cannot equal pending cases at the start of the

     because the order cannot be executed. This specific case type return to the stock, but cannot be measured in the system the
     public prosecution uses. Once those cases are assessed again and stream out, they become visible in the numbers in the
     system.
     Pending cases are cases that are yet to be judged and for which a hearing has to be planned. Cases for which the hearing has
     been planned, are not included in this number.

     Q107-1 (General Comment): Article 335 [Sentencing without trial - motion] -Criminal Code Procedure
     § 1. If the accused pleads guilty, and in the light of his explanations the circumstances of the commission of the offence and
     his guilt raise no doubts, and the attitude of the accused indicates that the objectives of the proceedings will be achieved,
     further proceedings may be omitted.
     The public prosecutor, instead of filing a bill of indictment, shall file a motion with the court for issuing a judgment of conviction
     at a hearing and for agreeing with the defendant on penalties or other measures envisaged for the offence charged, also
     taking into account the legally protected interests of the victim. The agreement may also include a specific decision on
     payment of legal costs.
     The public prosecutor may attach to the indictment a motion for a judgment of conviction to be handed down at a hearing and
     for the penalties or other measures prescribed for the offence charged to be agreed upon with the defendant, also taking into
     account the legally protected interests of the victim, if the circumstances of the offence and the defendant's guilt are beyond
     doubt, the evidentiary statements made by the defendant do not contradict the findings made, and the defendant's attitude
     indicates that the objectives of the proceedings will be achieved.
     *Article 156 of the Fiscal Penal Code, The public prosecutor, as well as the financial pre-trial body, may attach to the
     indictment a motion for issuing, without a hearing, a judgment of conviction and imposing a penalty or penal measure agreed
     with the accused for the fiscal offence or fiscal misdemeanour charged against him, if the circumstances of the commission of
     the offence do not raise any doubts and the attitude of the accused indicates that the objectives of the proceedings will be
     achieved.

     Q107 (2023): 3.1.3 Opportunism is not a feature of the Slovak legal system. Prosecutorial decisions are strictly bound by
     legality and officiality, with no discretion to decline prosecution if legal criteria are met. For the CEPEJ questionnaire, "NAP" is
     appropriate for the subcategory 'cases discontinued for reasons of opportunity'.
     Q107 (2022): It is necessary to state that the required table, or criteria, are different from our legal system. In our criminal
     proceedings, a large number of cases in the preliminary proceedings are closed by the investigator or police officer, while the
     table only requires cases closed by the prosecutor. In addition, matters terminated by the prosecutor may also be terminated
     by the so-called diversions in criminal proceedings, while the table only requires cases stopped by the prosecutor. The
     inconsistency of data with previous years is also caused by the fact that the prosecutor in the Slovak Republic has slightly
     different powers in the preliminary proceedings in contrast to the legal systems of other countries, so the data differ according
     to the point of view of the processor of the data.

     Q107 (General Comment): Methodology used: statistical data are kept on the accused, accused or convicted persons, and
     the data is related to the main crime per defendant (methodology as used in the Joint Annual Report on the Work of State
     Prosecutor's Offices and has been used in previous reports).
     IMPORTANT: Data also includes unfinished criminal complaintes against unknown perpetrators. It should be noted that on
     average, State Prosecutor's Offices receive between 30.000 and 60,000 complaints per year against unknown perpetrators.
     These are included in statistical data as unresolved cases until the perpetrator is discovered or the statute of limitations
     expires.
     1.Pending cases on 1 Jan. ref. Year: unresolved criminal complaints against known perpetrators (incl. adults, minors and legal
     entities) and unknown perpetrators.
     2. Incoming/received cases: criminal denunciations against known and unknown offenders.
     Criminal denunciations against known offenders include cases that were received by the prosecution office as cases with
     unknown offenders whose identity was discovered during the reporting period. Cases against known offenders are counted by
     the number of persons involved (i.e. a denunciation against five individuals is counited as five cases), cases against unknown
     offenders are counted by files.
     3. Processed cases: all resolved criminal complaints in the reporting year. There can be multiple criminal complaints in one
     case file, however the resolution is only one (for all complaints in one case file) – hence the difference between the sum of
     subcategories (3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4) and the actual number of resolved criminal complaints. The discrepancies in the numbers
     arise from the way cases are recorded in the information system: in general, in cases with multiple offences by one suspect
     typically there is a single resolution; in cases with multiple suspects with different offences cases may be split to allow different
     resolutions; in cases with same suspect and multiple complaints the cases may be merged.
     3.1.1 Discontinued by the public prosecutor because the offender could not be identified: the public prosecutor cannot
     discontinue a case, because the offender could not be identified.
     3.1.2 Discontinued by the public prosecutor due to the lack of an established offence or a specific legal situation: dismissed
     denunciations for other reasons than opportunity and accomplishing some tasks imposed or negotiated by state prosecutor.
     This category includes cases where prosecutor refrains from prosecution after the finish of judicial investigation.
     The great majority of cases against unknown offenders is dismissed because the pending time exceeds limitation period for
     criminal prosecution.
     In the case of proposed criminal offenses, the motion of the injured party is a procedural precondition for conducting criminal
     proceedings. If this presumption does not exist (it is no longer due to withdrawal), the legal consequence is rejection.
     For the most part, public prosecutors rejected complaints for other reasons, including cases in which it was not possible to
     continue the proceedings due to a lack of procedural or material preconditions (the act is not a criminal offense, there is no
     reasonable suspicion that the suspect committed a criminal offense (prosecuted ex officio), various procedural obstacles).
     3.1.3 Discontinued by the public prosecutor for reasons of opportunity
     Cases where denunciations were dismissed because the consequences of criminal prosecution would prove disproportionate
     to the weight of criminal offence and dismissed denunciations agains
     t minors because the proceedings against him/her would not be appropriate in view of the nature of the offence and
     circumstances in which it was committed, as well as in view of the past conduct of the minor and his personal traits.
     3.1.4 Discontinued for other reasons
     NAP - all data already covered in the above.
     3.2.Concluded by a penalty or a measure imposed or negotiated by the public prosecutor
     Dismissed denunciations due to concluded settlement between an offender and the aggrieved person or due to the offender
     accomplishing some tasks imposed by public prosecutor.
     3.3.Cases closed by the public prosecutor for other reasons
     NAP - all already covered in the above data.
     3.4.Cases brought to court
     Natural persons and legal entities charged before district and local courts and motions for punishment or educational measure
     for minors.
     4. Pending cases on 31 Dec. ref. year
     Unresolved criminal complaints as at 31 December of the previous year for all categories (adults, minors and legal entities).
     Inconsistencies within the table are possible due to the peculiarity of the IT system - it is a "live" system (dynamic reporting),
     meaning that the reported figures for a specific date or period of time inevitably vary for different reasons (e.g. the data was not
     promptly entered into the CMS; in some instances, the decision, in which category some specific new cases should be
     included, may be subsequently changed and when data are unified some figures change; there is also the possibility that a
     mistake was done when entering the data and was later detected in the quality check and corrected.). Every category (row in
     the table) is calculated (counted) separately, therefore the „Pending on 31 Dec“ may not equal to the formula (Pending 1 Jan +
     Incoming – Processed) due to aforementioned influences.

     Q107-1 (General Comment): The defendant may plead guilty in two kinds of situations. He/she can achieve an agreement
     with a state prosecutor in a plea-bargaining procedure or he/she can make a guilty plea irrespectively of the state prosecutor at
     the pretrial hearing and until the beginning of a main hearing. Cases brought to court by the public prosecutor through the
     guilty plea procedure are only first mentioned kind of cases. The agreement on guilty plea between the defendant and state
     prosecutor may be concluded before the commencement of the criminal proceedings and not later than by the beginning of the
     main hearing. There is no available data on the stage of the proceeding when the agreement was concluded.

     Q107-1 (2024): In 2024, the majority of plea negotiations were conducted in cases falling within the jurisdiction of the district
     courts and concerned serious criminal offences, often involving multiple defendants and requiring complex evidentiary
     proceedings. Increase in number of procedures: Approximately 40% of all plea agreements were concluded by a district
     prosecutor's office located in proximity to the state border, primarily in relation to offences of unlawful border crossing or
     irregular entry into the country, as defined in Article 308 of the Criminal Code-1.

     Q107-1 (2023): Compared to the previous year, there has been a 43% increase in the number of plea agreements. The
     increase in plea agreements is primarily due to crimes involving illegal border crossings.
     Q107-1 (2021): In the previous year (2020) the number of guilty plea procedures was unusually low due to two reasons: a
     stricter criminal framework (regarding illegal crossing of the state border or territory under Article 308 of the Criminal Code) and
     the impact of the Covid-19 pandemics.

     Q107-1 (2020): The reason for fewer negotiations and fewer agreements is mainly a stricter criminal framework for crimes that
     were still regulated in 2018 in such a way that they could be the subject of negotiations between the prosecutor and the
     defendant (illegal crossing of the state border or territory under Article 308 of Criminal Code). Due to the above, there was no
     interest on the part of the defendants as well as the state prosecutors to agree on guilt and criminal sanction as parties to
     criminal proceedings. In addition to this, an epidemiological reason for measures to prevent the spread of the covid-19
     epidemic is cited as the reason for the reduction in negotiations and plea agreements concluded, furthermore, the poor staffing
     situation and the high workload of state prosecutors who are engaged in urgent matters in the on-call service and in attending
     court hearings and the prompt announcement of pre-trial hearings shortly after the indictment becomes final, which
     significantly shortened the time for conducting negotiations and concluding a plea deal.

     Spain
     Q107 (General Comment): In Spain the general rule is that the Prosecutor is party in the criminal cases, but the Prosecutor
     does not process (with exclusive competence) the criminal cases. The investigation Judge (Juez de Instrucción) does that.
     Data provided in question 107 tries to adapt the information in the Annual Report of the State Attorney General's Office to the
     criteria of CEPEJ, by offering the data of cases received by the Prosecution Service, according to the classification of
     procedures of the Spanish procedural legislation (diligencias previas, diligencias urgentes, procedimiento por delitos leves,
     sumarios y procedimientos del jurado). In addition to that, there are other two kinds of actions for which the Prosecution have
     exclusive competence: Investigation of criminal reponsibility of minors, and preliminary diligences of Article 773.2 of the
     Criminal Procedural Act.
     Q107 (2020): The provided number of incoming cases is the number of the criminal proceedings received by the Prosecution
     Service (page 1117 of the Annual Report of the Prosecution Service). It is consistent with the explanatory note as it includes
     “cases submitted to public prosecutors by the police and other bodies as well as victims (if applicable) within the reference
     year”. It is an official data, provided by the State Attorney Office.
     Q107-1 (2021): Explanation of the increased number of guilty plea procedures: Probably, coming back to normal activity after
     covid restrictions.
     Q013 (General Comment): In Spain, it is very difficult to carry out a perfect separation between the budget of Courts and the
     Budget of Prosecution services, because some concepts are common (civil servants, material resources, buildings, etc).
     These items cannot be separated from the budget allocated to the functioning of courts. Therefore, the figure provided in
     respect of the “Total” represents only the salaries.
     It is noteworthy that data on the implemented budget is an estimations of the Statistic Department of the General Council of the
     Judiciary.

     Austria
     Q107 (General Comment): “3.1.3 Discontinued by the public prosecutor for reasons of opportunity”: discontinued
     investigations for reasons of opportunity are only counted by persons against which the investigation was discontinued. In one
     case, more than one person can be accused and the investigation can be discontinued for reasons of opportunity against more
     than one accused person. Therefore, the person-count was not delivered because it is inconsistent with the case-count (3.1.1,
     3.1.2 and 3.1.4). The number of cases in which an investigation was discontinued for reasons of opportunity is included in the
     number provided for 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 but cannot be evaluated separately with the standard statistic tools of the Federal Ministry
     of Justice of Austria.
     The provided number of cases discontinued for other reasons (3.1.4) contains cases discontinued because the offender is
     fugitive or an investigation may not be instituted or continued by law (e.g. because of diplomatic immunity of the offender), also
     cases (investigations) that were not instituted in the first place because the of a lack of an initial suspicion and all other cases
     that were discontinued but can not be allocated to one of the above mentioned reasons or the other reasons under 3.1.
     Under 3.3, closed cases against unidentified offenders were counted which were discontinued because of another reason than
     not identifying the offender in the end (mostly cases in which at least one formerly unidentified offender could be identified and
     therefore the case against the unidentified offender(s) is closed and another (new) case against the known offender(s) is
     opened).
     Following a change in Question 107, starting from 2022, cases previously reported as "closed for other reasons" are included
     in "discontinued for other reasons".

     Q107 (2020): The Austrian code of criminal procedure knows measures that the public prosecutor can take in cases of minor
     criminal offences (“Diversion”). Comparable measures have to be taken by the public prosecutor under certain circumstances
     under the addictive drug act (“Suchtmittelgesetz”). Until 2019, the last-mentioned cases were counted as files “discontinued by
     the public prosecutor due to the lack of an established offence or a specific legal situation” (3.1.2). Since 2020, these cases
     are now counted as “concluded by a penalty or a measure imposed or negotiated by the public prosecutor” (3.2). These
     changes explain the higher number of cases under 3.1.2. Cases brought to court declined mainly because in 2020 there were
     far less incoming cases (-13 % compared to 2018).
     The number of persons against which an investigation was discontinued by the public prosecutor for reasons of opportunity in
     2020 is 9 672.




     Belgium
     Q107 (General Comment): Data concerning the investigation and prosecution of criminal cases by the prosecutors' offices at
     the courts of first instance (http://www.om-mp.be/stat): tables 1, 6, 9 and 11.
     The data concern only criminal offences committed by persons of legal age. For “juvenile cases”, only data for incoming cases
     are available (no data available for resolved cases). Statistics on juvenile courts are currently being developed. Cases where
     the perpetrator is unknown are also included. The unit of account is a criminal case: a case may involve none, one or more
     defendants and/or one or more offences. Since the reform of the judicial landscape entered into force on 1 April 2014, Belgium
     has 15 first instance public prosecutors' offices (14 public prosecutors' offices + the Federal prosecutor's office). Data of the
     Federal prosecutor's office (FPO) are not included in the figures. The FPO prosecutes a limited list of offences set out in
     articles 144ter et seq of the Judicial Code. This list includes the following offences: crimes and offences against State security;
     threats of attack or theft of nuclear material; trafficking and organised trafficking in human beings; illegal arms trafficking;
     criminal conspiracy and criminal organisation; terrorism; offences related to these offences; offences which, to a large extent,
     concern several jurisdictions or which have an international dimension, in particular those of organised crime. Given the
     specific matters dealt with by the FPO and the low figures, the FPO data are not included in the figures provided. The FP0 data
     can be consulted separately on the Public Prosecutor's website: https://www.om-mp.be/stat/corr/jstat2022/n/home.html .
     Prior to 2022, “cases discontinued for other reasons” referred only to cases in which it was possible to determine from the
     database that they had been discontinued but the reason was not entered or was not correctly recorded. When the reason is
     correctly recorded, the case is then classified under headings 3.1.1, 3.1.2 or 3.1.3. As a result, the heading “discontinued for

     chambers (31,737 cases in 2020), summonses via accelerated procedure (1,159 cases in 2020) and correctionalizations (78

     within the framework of the settlement of the procedure (7,592 cases in 2020). A part of these referrals relates to cases that
     were initiated as a result of a civil action. Therefore, these cases were not initiated by the prosecution.
     The numbers of incoming, processed and pending cases have all increased for the same reason. Indeed, in 2020, the health
     crisis due to the outbreak of COVID-19 began. The government took measures to combat this crisis, including several periods
     of containment. The Public Prosecutor's Office was responsible for taking criminal action against non-compliance with these
     measures, which explains the sharp increase in the number of new cases and the fact that, at the same time, the flow of other
     types of cases did not decrease in the same proportions.
     Pending cases are cases that are being processed at a given time. If the inflow increases significantly, the number of pending
     cases will increase accordingly and reach a higher level.
     The increase in the "terminated with penalty" and "brought to court" headings is also related to the health crisis. The primary
     response to a COVID-19 non-compliance violation was a settlement (recorded under "terminated by pe
     nalty"). In the case of non-payment of the settlement, repeat offenses, or serious violations of these measures, the criminal
     policy was to bring the case to court, given the importance of compliance with these measures. About half of the increase in
     court cases is due to the new methodology. The other half is explained by citations in health crisis cases, as explained above.

     Q107 (General Comment): The following clarification is made on the specific indicators in the table:
     “1. 1.Pending cases on 1 Jan. ref. year” – This refers to pre-trial proceedings pending with the prosecutor on 1 January of the
     reference year, where the investigation has been completed by an investigating body and sent to the prosecutor. PTP not
     closed by an investigating authority are not included under this indicator.
     “2. Incoming/received cases” – Report the pre-trial proceedings for which an investigation by an investigative body was
     completed during the reference year and sent to the prosecutor for adjudication. The Prosecutor's Office reports as closed PTP
     cases with an investigation completed by an investigative body, not cases adjudicated by a prosecutor.
     “3. Processed cases” – For this indicator, the number indicated for PTP represents the number of PTPs disposed by a
     prosecutor. This number is formed as the sum of the number of cases decided by the PTP prosecutor (either by an act of
     referral to court or by an act of discontinuance of pre-trial proceedings) and the number of pre-trial proceedings decided by the
     prosecutor by an act of suspension or referral to another prosecutor's office. Cases suspended and sent to the prosecutor's
     office are counted as decided by the prosecutor's office, but provisionally, not on the merits. The prosecutor's act of
     suspending PTP does not constitute a decision on the merits, as it does not put an end to the criminal proceedings and the
     work on them is only suspended temporarily, i.e. they are not investigated by the investigating authority.
     With regard to the PTPs discontinued by the Prosecutor referred to under indicator “3.1. Discontinued during the reference
     year” the figure is formed by the sum of the data submitted under indicator “3.1.2. Discontinued by the public prosecutor due to
     the lack of an established offence or a specific legal situation”, including pre-trial proceedings terminated because the act was
     not committed or did not constitute a crime, as well as PTPs terminated due to statute of limitations; and the data submitted
     under indicator "3.1.4. Discontinued for other reasons”, reporting on PTPs discontinued/suspended and PTPs sent to the
     jurisdiction/sent by competence during the reporting period. The data on cases discontinued due to perpetrator of the crime not
     being identified are reported in indicator 3.1.4. This indicator (3.1.4.) reflects the total number of discontinued/suspended
     cases, without distinguishing between those discontinued due to failure to identify the perpetrator and those discontinued
     against a known perpetrator on other grounds. It should be borne in mind that PTPs suspended by limitation and PTPs sent to
     the competent prosecutor's office (by the sending prosecutor's office) are counted as PTPs resolved, so their number is
     included under the indicator 'Processed cases (3.1+3.2+3.3)', but not under the indicator 'Incoming/received cases '.
     Indicators “3.1.1. Discontinued by the public prosecutor because the offender could not be identified”, “3.1.3. Discontinued by
     the public prosecutor for reasons of opportunity” and 3.2. “Concluded by a penalty or a measure imposed or negotiated by the
     public prosecutor” are not applicable to prosecutors' rulings according to the CCP, and therefore no data are presented.
     “3.3. Cases brought to court” – This indicator takes into account the number of pre-trial proceedings brought to court with a
     prosecutor's report during the reference year.
     In the official statistical reporting of the PRB, a criminal case is reported as brought to cour




     t if at least one prosecutorial act has been submitted to the court – an indictment; a proposal for an agreement under Article
     381 of the Penal Procedure Code; a proposal for exemption from criminal liability and imposition of an administrative penalty
     under Article 78a of the Criminal Code, and a proposal for an agreement under Article 375a(1) of the Penal Procedure Code.
     However, more than one prosecutorial act may be submitted to the court in relation to a single pre-trial proceeding (e.g. an
     agreement in relation to one person and an indictment in relation to the other defendants). The prosecutorial acts submitted
     give rise to court cases in which prosecutors participate in court hearings, including when a proposal has been submitted to
     settle the case by agreement. A case is also opened in court, in which the prosecutor, the defendant and his defence counsel
     appear, and the court issues a judicial act. It should be noted that the official statistics of the PRB do not explicitly collect data
     on the number of pre-trial proceedings in which an indictment has been filed (the acts are counted, not the cases). Since there
     can only be one indictment per pre-trial proceeding, we have assumed that the number of pre-trial proceedings with an
     indictment is equal to the number of indictments. However, the official statistics of the PRB do not explicitly collect data on the
     number of pre-trial proceedings brought before the court with proposals for agreements under Article 381 of the Penal
     Procedure Code, proposals for exemption from criminal liability and imposition of administrative penalties under Article 78a of
     the Criminal Code, and proposals for agreements under Article 375a(1) of the Penal Procedure Code. In order to obtain this
     data, the number of pre-trial proceedings in which an indictment has been filed is subtracted from the total number of pre-trial
     proceedings brought before the court. Cases resolved by agreement or proposal under Article 78a of the Criminal Code can be
     indicated as a total number, without being able to distinguish them by type of prosecutorial act. “4. Pending cases on 31 Dec.
     ref. year” – This refers to PTPs remaining with the prosecutor for resolution as of 31 December of the reference year, where
     the investigation has been concluded by an investigating authority and sent to the prosecutor. The indicator does not include
     PTPs pending prosecution by an investigating authority as of 31 December.
     Regarding the cases sent by competence, the mathematical calculation for collecting the values is not applicable for the two
     prosecutor's offices - one that sent it by competence (according to the rules of local, functional or special competence), for
     which the case was decided “discontinued case for other reasons“ and the other, which accepted it within its competence, if at
     the end of the year the same case remained pending, the latter is included in the above data.

     Q107 (2024): The official statistics of the PORB also report and aggregate data on other indicators of pre-trial work that cannot
     be identified or do not match the indicators in the Questionnaire, therefore the following clarification is made:
     According to the reporting system introduced in the PORB, pretrial proceedings are reported as: Monitored, Closed (with
     investigation completed by investigating authority) and Resolved (by a prosecutor).
     Supervised pre-trial proceedings include: the newly initiated PTPs during the reporting period, in this case 2024 (89 145
     PTPs), the PTPs pending by an investigating authority at the end of the previous reporting period (57 495 PTPs), the PTPs
     pending by a prosecutor at the end of the previous reporting period (4 163 PTPs), the PTPs received under the jurisdiction
     during the reporting period, the PTPs returned by the court as well as by a prosecutor (incl. PTPs decided in previous periods
     but returned during the reporting period), PTPs reopened during the reporting period, PTPs merged (joined) and PTPs split.
     For statistical reporting purposes in the PORB (and not pursuant to the CCP), a pretrial proceeding is reported as resolved
     when any of the following prosecutor's decisions are made: a decree to send the PTP to the competent jurisdiction, a decree to
     suspend the PTP, a decree of discontinuance, a prosecutor's act to bring the case to court – indictment, a proposal for a
     settlement under Article 381 CCP, a proposal under Article 375 CCP, in conjunction with Article 78a CCP, for exemption from
     criminal responsibility with the imposition of an administrative penalty, and a proposal for a settlement under Article 375a(1)
     CCP.
     The statistical analysis distinguishes between the total number of cases decided in which one of the above-mentioned
     prosecutor's acts was handed down and the cases decided on the merits. Cases decided on the merits are only those decided
     by a decision to discontinue the criminal proceedings or by a prosecutor's act to bring the case to court, which concludes the
     pre-trial phase. PTPs decided by a decision to suspend and refer are not included as they do not end the pre-trial
     phase/criminal proceedings. PTPs sent to the jurisdiction are reported by the sending prosecutor's office as monitored PTPs
     and resolved PTPs, but are not reported as PTPs closed by the investigating authority. PTPs discontinued due to the expiry of
     the statutory limitation period (under Article 24(1)(3) CCP) shall be counted as PTPs observed and decided, but shall not be
     counted in the number of PTPs discontinued as they were already counted as such when they were discontinued. Suspended
     PTPs in previous periods are not counted in the total number of PTPs observed during the reference period, except in cases
     where the suspended PTP is resumed, where it is included in the number of PTPs observed and according to its current status
     at the end of the period.

     Q107 (2021): 3.1. Discontinued during the reference year (3.1.1+3.1.2+3.1.3+3.1.4.)
     The number of discontinued cases in the reference year (in the case of 2021) is 101626. This number includes all discontinued
     criminal proceedings by the prosecutor in the year on the basis of Art. 24 of the Criminal Procedure Code, including those
     terminated due to the expiration of the statute of limitations on the basis of Art. 24, para. 1, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure
     Code (criminal liability is extinguished due to the expiration of the statute of limitations).
     The number of cases terminated on statute of limitations grounds is a fact of objective reality, which does not depend on the
     prosecution. This number is a function of the number of the pending pre-trial proceedings, incl. suspended (predominantly due
     to failure to establish the perpetrator of the crime during the investigation), as well as the specific crime on which the case is
     being prosecuted, as the absolute statute of limitations for seeking criminal liability is different and depends on the amount of
     the penalty provided for in the Criminal Code for the relevant crime (according to Art. 81 of the Criminal Code).
     The increase in the number of dismissed cases for 2021 compared to those dismissed in 2020 is mainly due to the greater
     number of dismissed cases by the prosecutor on the grounds of absolute statute of limitations for prosecution, which obliges
     the prosecutor to dismiss the case on the basis of Art. 24, para. 1, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Code. This conclusion is
     supported by the statistical data for the two years - in 2021, the dismissed cases, on grounds other than the statute of
     limitations, are relatively similar: 32,400 for 2021 compared to 32,002 for 2020. However, those dismissed on statute of
     limitations grounds in 2021 are 69,226, and in 2020 - 42565. It can be seen that in 2021 the terminated pre-trial proceedings
     were significantly more than in the previous year. There is no evidence that this increase is due to any special or extraordinary
     circumstance that occurred in 2021. Each year the number of cases dismissed on statute of limitations grounds is different and
     this is due to the above reasons.

     Q107 (2024): In some cases indictment and subsequent discontinuation occurs within the same year. In such instances, a
     single case will both occur in both point 3.2 and 3.3. However, the case will only occur once when computing the total. Thus,
     the sum of 3.1-3.3 might not be the same as the total in 3.
     The reason for the discrepancy in closed/finished cases relative to incoming cases is that processed cases include cases that
     the prosecution service has responsibility for, but that both the police and prosecution service conducts work on – depending
     on the case. We cannot always distinguish closed/finished cases between the police and prosecution service as they are often
     archived in police departments regardless of who processed the case.
     One case accounts for one crime for each person involved in the crime. If two crimes were committed by three people, there
     would be six counts of crimes (=cases). Reports of crime might also grow in number of counts as it progresses through the
     chain of criminal proceedings. The ‘owner’ of the case is the department that last worked on it.
     The term “Reasons of opportunity” entails cases discontinued according to section 721, subsection 1, no. 3-4 of The Danish
     Administration of Justice Act, which is applied in cases where it is assed that legal costs and processing time are
     disproportionate in relation to the significance of the case and its potential sentence.
     It is correct that there has been an increase of approximately 83% when comparing 2024 to 2023. However, it is important to
     emphasize that these number cover individual offences rather than court cases they fall under. When comparing the number of
     court cases, where one or more offences have been discontinued due to reason of opportunity, we only see an ~18% increase.
     The reason behind this being that in 2024 a number of court cases, with a large number of individual offences, were settled
     with discontinuation. For instance; in 2024 five court cases had over 100 offences discontinued due to reason of opportunity –
     while another case had over 500 offences.
     Throughout 2024, there has been an increased effort in reducing the backlog of pending indictments, by prioritizing the
     processing of existing cases in court. Due to this prioritization, there has been a ~40% decrease in the number of pending
     indictments when comparing the beginning and end of 2024. However, this has also meant fewer resources allocated to
     initiating new prosecutions. The natural consequence being an increase in the number of pending charges.

     3.1.4 Discontinued for other reasons and 3.3. Cases closed by the public prosecutor for other reasons: The prosecutor must
     waive prosecution if: (1) the prerequisites for the bringing of charges provided in section 6, subsection 1 are not met; (2) the
     prosecutor waives prosecution on the basis of section 6, subsection 2; (3) the injured party has not requested that charges be
     brought or another special prerequisite provided in law for the bringing of charges referred to in section 2, subsection 2 is not
     met and the nature of the case requires that a separate decision be made. The prosecutor may waive prosecution if: (1) if no
     sentence more severe than a fine is to be anticipated for the offence and the offence, with consideration to its detrimental
     effects or the degree of culpability of the offender manifested in it, is to be deemed petty as a whole; and (2) if the suspect had
     not reached the age of eighteen at the time of the commission of the suspected offence and no sentence more severe than a
     fine or imprisonment for at most six months is to be anticipated for this offence and it is to be deemed to be more the result of
     lack of understanding or thoughtlessness than of heedlessness of the prohibitions and commands of the law. In addition, the
     prosecutor may waive prosecution, unless an important public or private interest requires otherwise if: 1) if criminal
     proceedings and punishment are to be deemed unreasonable or inappropriate in view of a settlement reached by the suspect
     in the offence and the injured party, the other action of the suspect in the offence to prevent or remove the effects of the
     offence, the personal circumstances of the suspect in the offence, the other consequences of the act to him or her, the welfare
     and health care measures undertaken and the other circumstances; (2) under the provisions on joint punishment or on the
     consideration of previous punishments in sentencing, the suspected offence would not have an essential effect on the total
     punishment; or (3) the expenses in continuing to consider the case would be in manifest disproportion to the nature of the case
     and to the sanction possibly to be expected in it. Also, If charges are being considered for two or more offences for which the
     same person is suspected and if he or she has contributed to the clarification of one or more of the suspected offences, the
     prosecutor may decide not to bring charges for all of the suspected offences. However, charges shall be brought if required by
     an important public or private interest.

     Germany
     Q107 (General Comment): Once per year, the Federal Statistical Office compiles and publishes the public prosecution
     statistic. Statistical ordinances define the scope and rules of data collection for these statistics. The public prosecution offices
     collect the data and submit it to the statistical offices of the federal states, who check and edit the data and send it to the
     Federal Statistical Office. In simplified terms, the statistical ordinance provides two different kinds of data collection sheets:
     The "procedural survey" that collects data on the specifics of the investigation proceedings carried out by the public
     prosecution and the "monthly survey" that collects data on the caseload and other workload of the public prosecution offices.
     The figures entered here do not include investigations against persons unknown. The public prosecution statistic only shows
     the number of charges filed against unknown perpetrators. Information on the further treatment of those charges is not
     available. This is because the monthly survey distinguishes between "caseload of investigation proceedings covered by the
     procedural surveys" and "other workload". Charges against persons unknown fall into the category “other workload”. The
     number of resolved and pending cases is only collected with regard to the first category (proceedings covered by the
     procedural surveys). If a suspect is identified in cases with an unknown perpetrator, the case receives a new file-number and
     then appears in the category "covered by the procedural surveys".

     Greece
     Q107 (General Comment): The data in the table are presented by case file (and not, for example, on the number of
     offenders). Vertical consistency in the table is not ensured because the data are continuously updated/corrected and because
     of unknown offender cases that are referred either to the investigating magistrate (when they are felonies) or to a preliminary
     procedure (when they are misdemeanors) have not yet been completed. All cases that are referred to the investigator are
     returned to the public prosecutor, whether the perpetrator is identified or not. Cases where the perpetrator could not be
     identified are considered as resolved, while the rest (where the perpetrator is identified) follow further criminal proceedings and
     are either solved within the reporting period or are considered pending in the next time period. More precisely, cases where the
     offender could not be identified are placed in the "unknown perpetrator file". Cases placed in the "unknown perpetrator file" are
     suspended with a decision of the prosecutor and such decisions are counted as “ 3.1.1 Discontinued by the public prosecutor
     because the offender could not be identified”.



     Q107 (2024): Source: Independent Department for the Collection and Processing of Judicial Statistical Data (JustStat).
     The observed increase in the number of cases discontinued for reasons of opportunity (+42%) and the number of cases
     referred to court (+30%) can be attributed to the reforms of the public prosecutor's office introduced in 2024. More specifically,
     under Law 5090/2024 prosecutors were given greater discretion to close cases when it is not in the public interest or when the
     offense is of low severity. This was applied more actively to misdemeanors, especially in cases with limited evidence or with
     conciliatory intentions.
     At the same time, the prosecution of crimes of domestic violence, organized crime, and corruption was strengthened, resulting

     recorded by the prosecution service has increased exponentially (+45.7%).

     increase (110.64%) – beyond the average increase detailed above – can be attributed to two cases. 1) In case no. 926/2021 of

     established that the suspect committed the crime [Section 398 (2) a) of the Criminal Procedure Code]).

     eight perpetrators, while the other perpetrators were subject to indictment.

     Q107 (2022): The data source - in accordance with the previous data provision - is The Statistical Subsystem of Completed
     Criminal Proceedings of the Unified Investigation Authority and Prosecution Service Criminal Statistics System (hereinafter
     ENyÜBS-BBS). In the ENyÜBS-BBS subsystem, the data is recorded when the investigating authorities or the Prosecution
     Service have made a procedural decision giving reasons for the provision of statistical data in connection with the crime (e.g.:
     dismissal of the criminal complaint, termination, suspension, accusation/indictment), relating to which statistical data was
     provided. Considering the time of data recording, the ENyÜBS-BBS subsystem is, therefore, of a so-called follow-up nature, so
     it does not show how many crimes occurred in the year under review, but it shows how many legal decisions were made in
     connection with such acts and in how many cases statistical data was provided in this context (in a registrative manner). As a
     result, the above also means that it may occur there is an ongoing criminal proceeding that is not included in the ENyÜBS
     database yet. For the questions "Pending cases on 1 Jan. ref. year" and "Pending cases on 31 December ref.year" in the
     table, please note that no data is collected on the number of pending cases – on a given day – into the records of the
     Prosecution Service. Set of data: ENyÜBS-BBS: number of criminal procedure decisions
     Unit of recording: criminal procedure decision
     Selection date: May 30, 2023.

     Q107 (2024): Increase in Cases Brought to Court (Section 3.3):
     In 2024, prosecutors took over 4,057 criminal proceedings involving particularly significant offenses. Compared to 2022, this
     represents a 40.3% increase. This rise is partly due to the reclassification of certain crimes as high-priority, such as violations
     of international and national sanctions, illegal border crossings, human smuggling, and facilitating unlawful residence in Latvia.
     Additionally, the number of cases submitted for prosecution involving these offenses increased significantly—from 454 in 2023
     to 975 in 2024—reflecting both improved investigative efforts and enhanced prosecutorial oversight.
     Decrease in Cases Concluded by Prosecutorial Penalty or Measure (Section 3.2):
     Contrary to previous years, where a growing number of cases were concluded within the prosecution, 2024 saw a notable
     decline. This shift is primarily due to amendments to the Criminal Law (effective July 4, 2024), which changed sentencing
     policies for certain categories of offenses—especially those involving violence or committed under the influence of alcohol or
     drugs in traffic incidents. These amendments removed alternative penalties such as community service and fines, leaving only
     probation supervision as an option. As a result, for offenses committed between July 4 and December 31, 2024, prosecutors
     could not conclude proceedings without referring the cases to court. This led to a significant increase in cases brought to court
     and a decrease in those resolved by prosecutorial penalty.

     Luxembourg
     Q107 (2024): 3.1.1 Between 2023 and 2024, a significant 26% increase was observed in resolved cases by the public
     prosecutor because the offender could not be identified. This development is part of a broader trend, marked by a continuous
     rise in the number of incoming cases registered by the public prosecutor’s offices in recent years. Since 2022, the proportion of
     cases with an unknown perpetrator has regularly exceeded 40% of the total cases handled.

     This situation is partly explained by the growing prevalence of cybercrime, which represents an increasing share of
     discontinued cases without further action. Prosecution in this area is particularly complex due to the technical nature of the
     offenses and their often international scope, making it difficult or even impossible to identify the perpetrators.

     Moreover, this increase also affects other categories of offenses, such as scams, frauds, and the intentional destruction or
     damage of movable property. In these cases as well, the absence of elements allowing for the identification of perpetrators
     prevents any judicial proceedings, thereby contributing to the rise in discontinued cases without further action.

     Q107 (General Comment): The number of pending cases at the end of the year cannot equal pending cases at the start of the
     year + incoming cases – processed cases, because a specific type of case can only be counted in the stock when the file has
     been judged, not when they are pending. This is for criminal cases where an order is given, but the case is then returned
     because the order cannot be executed. This specific case type return to the stock, but cannot be measured in the system the
     public prosecution uses. Once those cases are assessed again and stream out, they become visible in the numbers in the
     system.
     Pending cases are cases that are yet to be judged and for which a hearing has to be planned. Cases for which the hearing has
     been planned, are not included in this number.

CEPEJ study on the functioning of judicial systems

     Q107 (General Comment): Methodology used: statistical data are kept on the accused, accused or convicted persons, and
     the data is related to the main crime per defendant (methodology as used in the Joint Annual Report on the Work of State
     Prosecutor's Offices and has been used in previous reports).
     IMPORTANT: Data also includes unfinished criminal complaintes against unknown perpetrators. It should be noted that on
     average, State Prosecutor's Offices receive between 30.000 and 60,000 complaints per year against unknown perpetrators.
     These are included in statistical data as unresolved cases until the perpetrator is discovered or the statute of limitations
     expires.
     1.Pending cases on 1 Jan. ref. Year: unresolved criminal complaints against known perpetrators (incl. adults, minors and legal
     entities) and unknown perpetrators.
     2. Incoming/received cases: criminal denunciations against known and unknown offenders.
     Criminal denunciations against known offenders include cases that were received by the prosecution office as cases with
     unknown offenders whose identity was discovered during the reporting period. Cases against known offenders are counted by
     the number of persons involved (i.e. a denunciation against five individuals is counited as five cases), cases against unknown
     offenders are counted by files.
     3. Processed cases: all resolved criminal complaints in the reporting year. There can be multiple criminal complaints in one
     case file, however the resolution is only one (for all complaints in one case file) – hence the difference between the sum of
     subcategories (3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4) and the actual number of resolved criminal complaints. The discrepancies in the numbers
     arise from the way cases are recorded in the information system: in general, in cases with multiple offences by one suspect
     typically there is a single resolution; in cases with multiple suspects with different offences cases may be split to allow different
     resolutions; in cases with same suspect and multiple complaints the cases may be merged.
     3.1.1 Discontinued by the public prosecutor because the offender could not be identified: the public prosecutor cannot
     discontinue a case, because the offender could not be identified.
     3.1.2 Discontinued by the public prosecutor due to the lack of an established offence or a specific legal situation: dismissed
     denunciations for other reasons than opportunity and accomplishing some tasks imposed or negotiated by state prosecutor.
     This category includes cases where prosecutor refrains from prosecution after the finish of judicial investigation.
     The great majority of cases against unknown offenders is dismissed because the pending time exceeds limitation period for
     criminal prosecution.
     In the case of proposed criminal offenses, the motion of the injured party is a procedural precondition for conducting criminal
     proceedings. If this presumption does not exist (it is no longer due to withdrawal), the legal consequence is rejection.
     For the most part, public prosecutors rejected complaints for other reasons, including cases in which it was not possible to
     continue the proceedings due to a lack of procedural or material preconditions (the act is not a criminal offense, there is no
     reasonable suspicion that the suspect committed a criminal offense (prosecuted ex officio), various procedural obstacles).
     3.1.3 Discontinued by the public prosecutor for reasons of opportunity
     Cases where denunciations were dismissed because the consequences of criminal prosecution would prove disproportionate
     to the weight of criminal offence and dismissed denunciations agains
     t minors because the proceedings against him/her would not be appropriate in view of the nature of the offence and
     circumstances in which it was committed, as well as in view of the past conduct of the minor and his personal traits.
     3.1.4 Discontinued for other reasons
     NAP - all data already covered in the above.
     3.2.Concluded by a penalty or a measure imposed or negotiated by the public prosecutor
     Dismissed denunciations due to concluded settlement between an offender and the aggrieved person or due to the offender
     accomplishing some tasks imposed by public prosecutor.
     3.3.Cases closed by the public prosecutor for other reasons
     NAP - all already covered in the above data.
     3.4.Cases brought to court
     Natural persons and legal entities charged before district and local courts and motions for punishment or educational measure
     for minors.
     4. Pending cases on 31 Dec. ref. year
     Unresolved criminal complaints as at 31 December of the previous year for all categories (adults, minors and legal entities).
     Inconsistencies within the table are possible due to the peculiarity of the IT system - it is a "live" system (dynamic reporting),
     meaning that the reported figures for a specific date or period of time inevitably vary for different reasons (e.g. the data was not
     promptly entered into the CMS; in some instances, the decision, in which category some specific new cases should be
     included, may be subsequently changed and when data are unified some figures change; there is also the possibility that a
     mistake was done when entering the data and was later detected in the quality check and corrected.). Every category (row in
     the table) is calculated (counted) separately, therefore the „Pending on 31 Dec“ may not equal to the formula (Pending 1 Jan +
     Incoming – Processed) due to aforementioned influences.

     Spain
     Q107 (General Comment): In Spain the general rule is that the Prosecutor is party in the criminal cases, but the Prosecutor
     does not process (with exclusive competence) the criminal cases. The investigation Judge (Juez de Instrucción) does that.
     Data provided in question 107 tries to adapt the information in the Annual Report of the State Attorney General's Office to the
     criteria of CEPEJ, by offering the data of cases received by the Prosecution Service, according to the classification of
     procedures of the Spanish procedural legislation (diligencias previas, diligencias urgentes, procedimiento por delitos leves,
     sumarios y procedimientos del jurado). In addition to that, there are other two kinds of actions for which the Prosecution have
     exclusive competence: Investigation of criminal reponsibility of minors, and preliminary diligences of Article 773.2 of the
     Criminal Procedural Act.


     Q107 (2020): The provided number of incoming cases is the number of the criminal proceedings received by the Prosecution
     Service (page 1117 of the Annual Report of the Prosecution Service). It is consistent with the explanatory note as it includes
     “cases submitted to public prosecutors by the police and other bodies as well as victims (if applicable) within the reference
     year”. It is an official data, provided by the State Attorney Office.

     Croatia
     Q107-1 (General Comment): In criminal proceedings, the defendant is granted the right to plead guilty (for all or a number of
     the counts of the charge) and reach agreement on the sanction. If the defendant pleads guilty and no agreement on the
     sanction is reached, the panel shall confirm the indictment and a trial must be scheduled. The parties may negotiate on the
     conditions of pleading guilty and agreeing on a sanction. During these negotiations, the defendant shall have a defence
     counsel. If the president of the panel is served with a confirmed indictment to which the accused has pleaded guilty, the
     proposing of evidence for the trial shall be limited only to the evidence which concerns the decision on criminal-law sanctions.
     Where the accused pleads guilty to all counts of the charge, the president of the panel shall instruct him/her that he/she may
     immediately state his/her position on all the circumstances that incriminate him/her and present all the facts in his/her favour,
     after which the accused shall be interrogated. The guilty plea does not exempt the court from its duty to present other evidence
     as well. If the confession of the accused at the trial is complete and in accordance with the evidence already gathered, the
     court shall, in the course of evidentiary proceedings, present only those pieces of evidence that relate to the decision on
     punishment or other sanction. The State Attorney’s Office keeps only a track record on the judgments rendered by the court in
     the guilty plea procedure and no distinction can be made between the number of guilty plea procedures “before the court case”
     and their number “during the court case”.




     Q107-1 (2024): In response to question 107-1 (guilty plea procedure), information on judgments based on plea agreements
     was provided only under the "Before the main trial" section. The "During the main trial" section was marked as NAP (not
     applicable), as our legal system does not recognize a formal procedure for plea agreements during the trial. The reason for the
     increase relates to more frequent use of guilty plea procedures in 2024. The emphasis on utilizing such procedures stems from
     their ability to expedite court proceedings, enhance overall efficiency, and significantly reduce expenditures from the national
     budget."


     Q107-1 (2023): Regarding question 107-1 (guilty plea procedure), data on judgments based on the parties' agreement were
     entered only in the column "Before the main trial," while the column "During the main trial" was entered as NAP (not
     applicable) because our country lacks a formal institute for communication during the discussion.
     The stated discrepancy percentage of 21.77% can be attributed to the strike.

     * The data refer to cases under the jurisdiction of county state attorneys' offices and the Office for the Suppression of
     Corruption and Organized Crime
     **The data refer to cases under the jurisdiction of the municipal state attorney's offices, with a note that certain severe criminal
     cases are also under their jurisdiction, however, statistical data are presented in total for all criminal offenses under the
     jurisdiction of the municipal state attorney's offices without separating them into "lighter" and "serious" crimes.
     The number of agreements from municipal jurisdiction was 318 in 2022, and 242 in 2021, which represents a true increase of
     31%. There is no particular reason for this increase, as it is a number that varies depending on the specifics of each reporting
     period (for example, it was 190 in 2018, 2019 -315, 2020 -266, 2021 -242 and 2022 -318). In fact, it is about the decisions of
     the court that should accept the agreement proposal submitted jointly by the state attorney's office and the defence. The State
     Attorney's Office strives to increase the number of agreements concluded every year in order to shorten court proceedings and
     relieve the work of the State Attorney's Office and the court, which is why the number of judgments based on the parties'
     agreement is monitored and analysed. However, the state attorney's office tries to maintain an appropriate criminal policy and
     insists on compensation for damages for victims, which is why the state attorney's office's proposals for agreements are not
     acceptable for defence in conditions of slow trials due to the significant workload of the courts, and realistically the number of
     agreements is not high. For this reason, data on the number of verdicts based on agreements in the annual report of the State
     Attorney's Office of the Republic of Croatia are considered in relation to the total number of convictions. In 2022, agreements
     from municipal jurisdiction accounted for 2.19% of the total number of convictions from municipal jurisdiction, which is only a
     slight increase of 0.62% compared to 2021, when agreements accounted for 1.68% of the total number of convictions % which
     actually does not represent a significant difference and is therefore not commented on.

     Finland
     Q107-1 (General Comment): The possibility of plea bargaining was introduced to the Finnish legal system in the beginning of
     year 2015. The aim of the reform was to allocate the resources of the national authorities in a more effective way and to speed
     up both the pre-trial phase of the criminal process and the court proceedings. A defendant can agree to plead guilty to a
     particular charge in exchange for a more lenient sentence. The prosecutor may also decide not to prosecute for one or for
     several of the suspected crimes. Plea bargaining can be used if the injured party has no demands in the matter and if he/she
     agrees to plea bargaining. Plea bargaining can be used when a person is suspected of a crime carrying a maximum sentence
     of six years' imprisonment. It cannot be used for crimes like homicide, causing bodily injury and sex offences or when the
     injured party is a child. Plea bargain is also applicable for white-collar crimes.



     Q107-1 (2022): Data on guilty plea procedure is not comprehensive. The procedure is registered in information systems only in

     this.

     France
     Q107-1 (General Comment): Appearance on prior recognition of guilt (CRPC) is a simplified prosecution procedure. The
     public prosecutor can propose to any adult offender who acknowledges the facts attributed to them to serve one or more of the
     penalties they face. This procedure applies to offenses (délits) except for exceptions provided by law (see Article 495-7 of the
     Code of Criminal Procedure). In case of acceptance of the proposed penalties, the public prosecutor refers the case to the
     judge to approve the accepted penalties. The approval order has the effect of a conviction judgment. It is recorded in the
     National Criminal Record.
     The CRPC is considered a full hearing (the judge wears a robe, and renders an "order" accepting the sentence — though not a
     judgment). The penalty imposed will carry the same weight as if it had been imposed during a "regular" hearing. However, if
     the individual refuses the penalty during this process, the prosecutor will redirect the case to a regular criminal trial. If the
     CRPC is successful, it will be considered the "main judicial procedure." However, if it fails, the individual will be presented
     before the criminal court, meaning the CRPC can be seen as a procedure that happens "before the main trial" In this sense,
     during a CRPC, the individual is not subject to "formal prosecution" before the court, but rather summoned before the
     prosecutor who offers them a penalty, which may or may not be accepted, and later approved or not by a judge.



     Q107-1 (2024): These figures correspond only to the CRPC: Appearance on prior recognition of guilt.
     It is a simplified prosecution procedure. The public prosecutor can propose to any adult offender who acknowledges the facts
     attributed to them to serve one or more of the penalties they face. This procedure applies to offenses (délits) except for
     exceptions provided by law (see Article 495-7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). In case of acceptance of the proposed
     penalties, the public prosecutor refers the case to the judge to approve the accepted penalties. The approval order has the
     effect of a conviction judgment. It is recorded in the National Criminal Record.

     Greece
     Q107-1 (General Comment): The accused who is usually a temporary prisoner but whose case is pending before the
     investigating judge, requests, either through his/her counsel or himself/herself (through an ex officio counsel) the criminal
     negotiation of his/her case. This request is forwarded to the Prosecutor's Office of Appeal to which copies of the relevant file
     are sent. Depending on the case, the appeal prosecutor will either recommend that the case be successful or unsuccessful. In
     the first case, if the case succeeds, a trial date is set at which the defendant appears before the court (Court of Appeal) and is
     given the proposed sentence. If he or she agrees, the procedure is completed and in most cases the defendant is released
     and the time spent in temporary custody is taken into account. If the defendant does not agree with the sentence proposed,
     the defendant withdraws his/her request for criminal negotiation, the proceedings are considered as not having taken place,
     and the defendant's criminal treatment continues from the point of the request for criminal negotiation.

     Q107-1 (2024): Source: Independent Department for the Collection and Processing of Judicial Statistical Data (JustStat)
     The violations of restrictive measures that led to mass registrations and quick guilty pleas in 2021–2022 no longer exist,
     resulting in a natural decrease in related cases. However, additional factors in 2024 contributed to this trend, including reforms
     of the prosecution service under Law 5090/2024, stricter criteria for accepting guilty pleas, increased use of the principle of
     opportunity, and the expansion of alternative dispute resolution mechanisms. More specifically, the new Criminal Code
     introduced stricter criteria for accepting guilty pleas, especially in cases involving social disapproval or domestic violence.
     The strengthening of the opportunity principle has led to more cases being shelved rather than confessions being accepted.
     The promotion of criminal mediation and out-of-court settlements has reduced the need for formal guilty plea procedures.

     were banned at that time, social events e.g. weddings were held in some areas of the country. In these cases, the guests (who
     may have exceeded, for example, 100) were brought before, for example, the public prosecutor who, in application of Article

     Hungary
     Q107-1 (2024): Discrepancy explanation:
     Based solely on data analysis, it can be stated that the number of defendants affected by final court decisions decreased by
     3.8% in 2024 compared to the previous year (2,156 defendants). Thus, as can be seen from the other data sets, there has
     been a general decrease in the number of defendants.
     If we examine the ratios of the two legal institutions (acceptance of confessions made at preparatory hearings; acceptance of
     confessions made at first instance trials), a kind of restructuring can be observed.
     In 2023, compared to all defendants affected by final judgments, the acceptance of confessions made at the preparatory
     hearing by the court accounted for 21.4%, while the acceptance of confessions made at the first instance trials by the court
     accounted for 2.2% of the cases. The same figures for 2024 were 21.9% and 1.7%, respectively. It can therefore be concluded
     from the above that although the number of defendants decreased in both data sets, proportionally more defendants made
     confessions and had them accepted by the court during the preparatory proceedings than during the first instance trial.
     Thus, it can be concluded that, looking solely at the ratios, proportionally more defendants made confessions during the
     preparatory proceedings, which were accepted by the court, and this presumably led to a decrease in the number of
     defendants who made confessions during the first-instance trial.
     In general, the prosecution service has no influence on how many defendants make confessions during court proceedings in a
     given year, or at what stage of the proceedings they do so.

     Q107-1 (General Comment): Article 335 [Sentencing without trial - motion] -Criminal Code Procedure
     § 1. If the accused pleads guilty, and in the light of his explanations the circumstances of the commission of the offence and
     his guilt raise no doubts, and the attitude of the accused indicates that the objectives of the proceedings will be achieved,
     further proceedings may be omitted.
     The public prosecutor, instead of filing a bill of indictment, shall file a motion with the court for issuing a judgment of conviction
     at a hearing and for agreeing with the defendant on penalties or other measures envisaged for the offence charged, also
     taking into account the legally protected interests of the victim. The agreement may also include a specific decision on
     payment of legal costs.
     The public prosecutor may attach to the indictment a motion for a judgment of conviction to be handed down at a hearing and
     for the penalties or other measures prescribed for the offence charged to be agreed upon with the defendant, also taking into
     account the legally protected interests of the victim, if the circumstances of the offence and the defendant's guilt are beyond
     doubt, the evidentiary statements made by the defendant do not contradict the findings made, and the defendant's attitude
     indicates that the objectives of the proceedings will be achieved.
     *Article 156 of the Fiscal Penal Code, The public prosecutor, as well as the financial pre-trial body, may attach to the
     indictment a motion for issuing, without a hearing, a judgment of conviction and imposing a penalty or penal measure agreed
     with the accused for the fiscal offence or fiscal misdemeanour charged against him, if the circumstances of the commission of
     the offence do not raise any doubts and the attitude of the accused indicates that the objectives of the proceedings will be
     achieved.
